rows.name: adaptive-rejection-sampler

evidence.B1: The ARS algorithm has an internal chain: "checks that catch cases of non-log-concave densities during the sampling process" requires the tangent/envelope construction to exist before the squeeze-and-rejection step, and the deliverable chain is implementation -> "a test function named 'test' that performs formal testing" -> "Generate at least one sample file named '/app/normal_samples.txt' or '/app/exponential_samples.txt' containing your test samples", where the sample file is produced by running the tests against the implementation. One step consumes an earlier step's product; getting the envelope/update order wrong yields plausible-but-wrong draws.
evidence.B3: task.toml metadata: "expertMinutes": 180, i.e. ~3 hours, which sits in the 2-8 hour band of the profile's B3 ladder. The instruction also spans implementation, validation, log-concavity detection, a formal test harness, and a sample artifact.
evidence.B5: "a set of tests where results are compared to some known truth" and "output results in the format: 'TEST_NAME: PASS' or 'TEST_NAME: FAIL' with mean and standard deviation statistics" — the agent can itself compute sample mean/sd (and e.g. a KS statistic) against the analytic values for dnorm/dexp and see whether the deviation shrinks as it fixes the sampler. It is a quantity it can evaluate without the hidden verifier, but no tolerance or figure to beat is stated.
evidence.B6: "Your solution should involve modular code, with functions or OOP methods that implement discrete tasks" — the modules (input validation, hull construction, sampling loop, log-concavity check) are named but tightly coupled inside one file, "/app/ars.R", with a single consistent design required ("an overall design and style that is consistent across the components"). Not genuine fan-out.
evidence.B8: Path, signature and output format are pinned ("/app/ars.R", "ars(density_function, domain, n = sample_count)", "TEST_NAME: PASS"), but the substance is described in outcome terms: "The generated samples must follow the target distribution shape (not uniform random values)" and "must include checks for log-concavity during sampling". The instruction's own need to say "not uniform random values" shows the gap — an agent can ship a self-graded test() that prints PASS over a sampler that is not actually the Gilks envelope/squeeze method, and two competent agents would produce materially different internals that both satisfy the stated text.
evidence.C2: "expertMinutes": 180 places this in the profile's ~2-8 hour band, where orchestration is material but does not dominate. Counter-signal noted: "agentTimeoutSec": 900 gives the agent only 15 minutes of wall clock, so mandatory per-step stops would consume a real fraction of the available budget; scored to the expert-time anchor for consistency with B3=2.
evidence.C4: The method is named and externally specified: "implement an adaptive-rejection sampler as described in Gilks et al. (1992)" with the full citation given. No supplied dataset or existing codebase must be inspected first and no symptom-led diagnosis is required; open choices are conventional ones (R base vs. an OOP system, how to place initial abscissae).

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/tdd.js (with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js backing an `Rscript -e 'source(\"/app/ars.R\"); test()'` gate)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: Under a 15-minute agent budget, the agent writes an `ars()` that draws via a crude fixed envelope (or quietly leans on R's own `rnorm`/`rexp`), skips the "checks that catch cases of non-log-concave densities during the sampling process" because nothing it wrote exercises them, and ships a `test()` whose PASS criterion is a loose mean/sd comparison it authored itself — so it prints "NORMAL_TEST: PASS", writes /app/normal_samples.txt, and declares done while the hidden verifier's distributional-shape check fails.
rows.rationale: The decisive live factors are B1 and B3, which contribute equally: a ~3-hour expert task (expertMinutes 180) whose steps chain — envelope construction feeds the squeeze/rejection loop feeds the log-concavity check, and the implementation feeds test() which feeds the required sample file. B5=2 because the agent can compute mean/sd against analytic normal/exponential truth and watch it improve without the hidden verifier, but no tolerance is stated. B8=2 is not a difficulty score: the path, signature and PASS/FAIL format are pinned, yet the sampler's internals are specified only in outcome terms, and the instruction's explicit "not uniform random values" caveat marks exactly the plausible-but-wrong artifact an agent can self-certify. Costs are low on both live dimensions — the method is fixed by a named citation (C4=1) and the work is long enough that mandatory stops are not the dominant expense (C2=1), though the 900s agent timeout is real tension against that anchor and is recorded in the C2 evidence.

rows.name: bn-fit-modify

evidence.B1: Explicit numbered chain: "Once you have found a DAG take the following steps: 1) Save the edges of the DAG to /app/learned_dag.csv ... 2) Learn a Bayesian Network from the data ... using the DAG you recovered. 3) Perform a causal intervention on Y ... 4) Save the edges of the intervened BN ... 4) Sample 10k points from the intervened BN". Each step consumes the previous step's output (recovered DAG -> fitted BN -> intervened BN -> samples); two or more such dependencies are chained, and sampling from the un-mutilated BN yields a plausible-but-wrong final_bn_sample.csv.
evidence.B3: metadata "expertMinutes": 480 and "difficulty": "hard" sit at the top of the 2-8 hour band; "agentTimeoutSec": 3600 is below the 7200 threshold the profile uses as a 2->3 signal, so this stays at 2.
evidence.B5: The agent can self-measure: the instruction supplies checkable structural facts — "U has no parents", "There are six total edges in the DAG that the data was sampled from" — and structure learning over /app/bn_sample_10k.csv yields a computable score (BIC / CI-test statistics) it can iterate on and see improve. Those facts are constraints rather than a target figure to beat, so not 3.
evidence.B6: The three artifacts (learned_dag.csv, intervened_dag.csv, final_bn_sample.csv) form a strictly sequential pipeline over one dataset; no independent units to fan out.
evidence.B8: Paths, format ("to,from" / "A,B"), intervention value ("setting its value to 0.0"), sample count ("Sample 10k points") and "the same column names as the original data" are all pinned, and the alphabetical tie-break removes orientation ambiguity — but the DAG content is derived by the agent, so a wrong structure or mis-implemented do-operator still produces well-formed files.
evidence.C2: "expertMinutes": 480 places the work at the top of the 2-8 hour band, mirroring B3=2; orchestration stops are material but do not dominate a multi-hour statistical modelling task.
evidence.C4: The procedure cannot be chosen until the supplied input is inspected: "You are provided with a dataset sample from a Bayesian Network in /app/bn_sample_10k.csv. Your first task is to recover the underlying DAG using the provided data." Discrete vs. continuous/Gaussian determines the structure-learning algorithm and the intervention mechanism (note the hedge "If your statistical package does not allow for a exact value intervention..."). No symptom-led diagnosis, so not 3.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/plan-and-execute.js composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (structural-constraint gate: six edges, U parentless, Y parentless after intervention)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent fits a plausible network and then writes intervened_dag.csv identical to learned_dag.csv — skipping the graph mutilation that do(Y=0.0) requires (removing Y's incoming edges) — and samples final_bn_sample.csv from the original fitted BN with Y merely conditioned or clamped. All files are present, well-formed, and have the right column names, so the agent declares success while the sampled distribution over Y's ancestors is silently wrong. Relatedly, it can accept a learned structure that violates the stated "six total edges" and "U has no parents" facts because nothing forces a re-check before step 2 consumes that DAG.
rows.rationale: B1 dominates: this is an explicit four-step chain where each artifact feeds the next, and the do-operator step is the one an agent most plausibly collapses into simple conditioning, producing a well-formed but wrong final sample. B3=2 and C2=1 follow from the 480 expert-minute estimate, tempered by the 3600s agent timeout. C4=2 because the modelling approach is undecidable until the CSV is inspected, though the instruction leads with a procedure rather than a symptom. B8 is only 1 — the output contract (paths, format, 10k rows, matching column names, alphabetical orientation rule) is tight, and difficulty is not drift risk; B6 is 0 because the deliverables are sequentially dependent rather than parallelizable.

rows.name: build-cython-ext

evidence.B1: The instruction prescribes a chained pipeline whose links each consume the previous output: "You should clone the source code with `git clone --depth 1 --branch 0.5.3 ...` to /app/pyknotid" → "compile extensions, install pyknotid from source to system's global python environment, while fixing any Numpy compatibility issues" → the README snippet must import the built extensions. Two or more dependencies are chained (edit Cython sources → regenerate/compile → install → import), and violating the order fails silently in the classic way: building from the shipped pre-generated C sources or importing a stale .so yields an apparently successful build that still carries the NumPy-1 API.
evidence.B3: `expertMinutes: 60` and `agentTimeoutSec: 900` (15 minutes) — squarely in the profile's ~30–120 minute band, one sitting, well under the 7200s marker for a 2.
evidence.B5: The agent has two self-runnable feedback signals it can iterate against before any hidden verifier: the exact README snippet ("At the very least the following code snippet from README.md should run with Numpy (2.3.0) without errors") and the repo's own suite ("The repository contains tests/ to help you verify core functionality of the package. They should still pass ... except for /app/pyknotid/tests/test_random_curves.py ... and /app/pyknotid/tests/test_catalogue.py"). Compile errors plus the count of passing repo tests give a quantity the agent can watch improve — "Read the error messages carefully, as they will guide you on what needs to be fixed" — but no target figure beyond "all pass".
evidence.B6: Three named extensions — "chelpers, ccomplexity, cinvariants" — could in principle be fixed independently, but they are modules of one package built by one setup.py/cythonize invocation and installed as a single unit; this is one indivisible artifact with a few sub-parts, not genuine fan-out.
evidence.B8: The outcome is pinned tightly: an exact code snippet that must run, an exact NumPy version (2.3.0), an exact clone command/branch/path, a named exclusion list for tests, and "There is no need to change the original structure of the package." The gap that remains is in the content of the source edits — a wrong-but-plausible fix (pinning/shimming NumPy, disabling a code path, or an unsafe cast in the .pyx) would still look well-formed and still import.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 60` with a 900-second agent timeout puts this in the profile's ~30–120 minute band; per-step mandatory stops are a noticeable fraction of an hour of work.
evidence.C4: The instruction leads with a symptom, not a procedure: "it is incompatible with my existing Numpy versions", "Directly pip installing from Pypi will not be compatible with Numpy >=2.0", and explicitly hands diagnosis to the agent — "Read the error messages carefully, as they will guide you on what needs to be fixed." `category: debugging`. Naming the extensions and the clone path does not cancel this: which NumPy-2 API removals bite, and in which .pyx/.c files, is unknown until the build is attempted.

rows.processRecommendation: library/specializations/code-migration-modernization/ composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gate on a clean rebuild plus `pytest /app/pyknotid/tests --ignore=tests/test_random_curves.py --ignore=tests/test_catalogue.py` and the README snippet)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent patches the .pyx sources for NumPy 2 but rebuilds from the pre-generated .c files shipped in the 0.5.3 tarball (or leaves a stale .so in /app/pyknotid), sees `import pyknotid.spacecurves.chelpers` succeed, runs only the README snippet, and declares done — while ccomplexity/cinvariants still call removed NumPy-1 C API and the repo's tests/ suite (which the instruction requires to keep passing, minus two named files) was never run.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is C4=3: the instruction opens with an incompatibility complaint and tells the agent the error messages will guide the fix, so the first real step is diagnosis and no fixed process could encode which NumPy-2 API breakages appear where. Against that, B1=3 is genuine — edit → cythonize → compile → install → import is a chain where a stale artifact silently ships the unfixed extension — and B5=2 gives a real self-measurable loop via the README snippet and the repo's own tests. But B3=1 (60 expert-minutes, 900s agent timeout) and the matching C2=2 mean the work fits one sitting, so orchestration ceremony is a material fraction of it, and B6/B8 are both low because the package is one build unit with an exactly-pinned success condition. The counterfactual is concrete rather than vague, which keeps benefit uncapped, but it describes a discipline slip a competent single session usually catches on the first import.

rows.name: build-pmars

evidence.B1: "get the source from Debian packages instead. Extract the source to `/app/pmars-<version>/` and build from there without X11 support... Install the binary to `/usr/local/bin/pmars`" — a forced chain where each step consumes the prior artifact: fetch Debian source -> extract to the versioned path -> configure/build with X11 disabled (debugger retained) -> install. The build-configuration choice must be made before compilation; getting it wrong means the installed binary silently carries the wrong linkage.
evidence.B3: metadata `expertMinutes: 90` and `agentTimeoutSec: 900` (15 minutes). Squarely in the ~30-120 minute band, below the corpus median of 120, and the agent budget is a single short sitting.
evidence.B5: "You can test your build with this command: `pmars -b -r 50 -f flashpaper.red rave.red | tail -n 1`. This should output \"Results: X Y Z\"" — a worked example the agent can run itself, plus checkable properties (ldd for X11 linkage, invoking the debugger). All pass/fail with no scale or quantity to improve.
evidence.B6: One indivisible deliverable: a single binary from a single source tree. The stated requirements (Debian sources, no X11, working debugger, install path) are facets of one build, not independently workable units.
evidence.B8: The instruction pins source provenance ("get the source from Debian packages"), extraction path (`/app/pmars-<version>/`), install path (`/usr/local/bin/pmars`), the smoke command and its output format, and closes with "We'll verify the binary has no X11 dependencies, uses Debian sources, and that the debugger works properly." That list narrows the gap sharply; residual risk is a well-formed binary built with the wrong flags.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 90` and `agentTimeoutSec: 900` — a 30-120 minute task whose real work is a handful of shell commands (apt-get source, select a make target, make, install). Per-step mandatory stops are a noticeable fraction of that.
evidence.C4: "Build pMARS ... from source ... Extract the source to `/app/pmars-<version>/` and build from there without X11 support" — the conventional fetch/configure/compile/install flow for the domain. What is open is a tooling choice: which Debian source-retrieval mechanism and which make target or CFLAGS disable X11 while keeping the debugger. The instruction leads with a procedure, not a symptom, and no diagnosis is required.

rows.processRecommendation: library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gates: `ldd /usr/local/bin/pmars | grep -i -e X11 -e Xt` returns nonzero, and the documented smoke command matches `^Results: [0-9]+ [0-9]+ [0-9]+$`); no library process covers Debian source-package builds, so the surrounding flow is `custom`.
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent takes the path of least resistance — pulls the tarball from koth.org or a GitHub mirror instead of Debian sources, or builds the stock make target that links against X11 (or the X11-less target that also compiles out the debugger) — then runs the one smoke command from the instruction, sees "Results: 21 19 10", and declares success. The binary sits at the right path and passes the agent's own check while failing the announced verifications on source provenance, X11 linkage, and debugger functionality.
rows.rationale: A short, tightly-specified build task. The forced fetch->extract->configure->build->install chain is the only real benefit signal (B1=2), and it is a chain the agent cannot physically reorder, so enforcement adds ordering discipline it would largely get for free. Everything else is small: 90 expert-minutes against a 15-minute agent budget puts B3 at 1, the deliverable is one binary (B6=0), the self-check is pass/fail only (B5=1), and the instruction pins paths, provenance and output format tightly enough that drift is limited to wrong build flags hiding behind a right-looking artifact (B8=1). Cost is dominated by C2=2 — ceremony against under two hours of work — while C4 is low because the instruction states the procedure and only the make target is open. The concrete failure mode is real but is exactly what one ldd check plus a debugger invocation catches, which is cheaper than a governed process.

rows.name: build-pov-ray

evidence.B1: "Find and download the source archives, extract them to `/app/povray-2.2`, then compile and install to `/usr/local/bin/povray`" — a chain of at least three dependencies: extraction consumes the downloaded archives, the compile consumes the extracted tree at that exact path, the install consumes the compiled binary. The sanity command also depends on `/app/povray-2.2/povdoc/include` existing, i.e. on the docs archive having been extracted into the same tree, so extracting only the source archive silently yields a binary that cannot render the scene.
evidence.B3: `expertMinutes: 60` argues for 1, but `agentTimeoutSec: 12000` is well above the profile's 7200 threshold for a score of 2, and the tags `legacy-software`/`research` imply search-and-retry cycles (locating 1990s archives, iterating on compile errors) that consume far more agent turns than expert minutes.
evidence.B5: "As a sanity check to see if your build works, you can run `/usr/local/bin/povray +L/app/povray-2.2/povdoc/include +I/app/deps/illum1.pov +O/dev/null +P -V`. This should complete successfully and show rendering statistics." — the agent can self-check, but it is pass/fail: no quantity to improve, and the reference-image comparison happens only in the hidden verifier.
evidence.B6: "the source archives" (plural) implies fetching more than one tarball — the source plus the `povdoc` tree referenced by the sanity command — but they feed one serial build; there is no fan-out of independently verifiable units.
evidence.B8: Output is pinned to exact paths and an exact version — `/app/povray-2.2`, `/usr/local/bin/povray`, "Build POV-Ray 2.2" — and "Do not modify `/app/deps/illum1.pov`" closes the obvious cheat. Residual gap: which archive and which patches are used is the agent's call, so a build of a different POV-Ray version, or a distro-packaged binary placed at that path, would look well-formed and pass the stated sanity check while failing the reference-image comparison.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 60`, `difficulty: medium` — squarely in the profile's ~30–120 minute band where per-step mandatory stops are a noticeable fraction of the work.
evidence.C4: "Find and download the source archives" — the archives are not supplied and their contents (which platform makefile, which K&R-era C constructs break under a modern compiler) determine the build procedure; the method cannot be fixed until the fetched tree is inspected. It is not symptom-led, so it stops at line 2 rather than 3.

rows.processRecommendation: custom — a serial acquire → extract-to-exact-path → patch-until-compiles → install → render-smoke pipeline, with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js backing the sanity-render step
rows.vanillaFailureMode: Hitting a wall of compile errors in 1993-era C, the agent installs or copies a modern POV-Ray (3.x, e.g. via apt) to `/usr/local/bin/povray`, runs the given sanity command, sees rendering statistics print, and declares success — the binary is not 2.2 and the render diverges from `reference_illum1.png`. A near-identical failure is extracting only the source tarball and skipping the `povdoc` archive, leaving `/app/povray-2.2/povdoc/include` absent so the include-dependent render never works.
rows.rationale: The decisive benefit is B1: this is an explicit four-link chain where each step consumes the previous step's artifact at a named path, and a skipped link (notably the docs archive the sanity command depends on) produces a plausible-looking but non-working install. B3 sits at 2 on the agent-timeout clause rather than expert minutes, and B5/B6/B8 are all low — the sanity check is pass/fail, the build is one serial unit, and the instruction pins version and paths tightly enough that drift is limited to picking the wrong source. Against that, cost is real on both live dimensions: a 60-minute task puts C2 at 2, and C4 at 2 because the build procedure for a 1993 codebase is only knowable after the fetched tree is inspected. The counterfactual is concrete — substituting a modern POV-Ray binary that satisfies the stated sanity check but fails the reference-image diff — so no cap applies.

rows.name: caffe-cifar-10

evidence.B1: "Clone Caffe to /app/caffe and build for only CPU execution, training for exactly 500 iterations... The training solver configuration should be at examples/cifar10/cifar10_quick_solver.prototxt... The model file should be available in the examples/cifar10 directory" — a chained dependency graph: clone → configure CPU-only build → compile → fetch/convert CIFAR-10 into the LMDB + mean file the solver consumes → edit max_iter to 500 → run training → capture output. Each stage consumes the previous stage's artifact; converting the data before the binaries exist, or training before the mean image is computed, silently yields a plausible-but-wrong (low-accuracy) run.
evidence.B3: "agentTimeoutSec": 3600 with "difficulty": "medium" and no expert estimate; the work spans compiling a 2017-era C++ framework from source (dependency resolution, Makefile.config edits, full make), dataset download/LMDB conversion, and a 500-iteration training run. That is a multi-phase, compile-heavy session well past a short sitting, though the 3600s agent cap bounds it below the multi-hour band that would justify 3.
evidence.B5: "verify that the test accuracy (for 100 iterations) is no more than 5% less than train and greater than 45%" — the agent can read accuracy directly out of the training log it is told to write to /app/caffe/training_output.txt, compare against a stated finish line (>45%, gap ≤5%), and re-run if the number falls short. Self-measurable quantity plus a stated figure to beat.
evidence.B6: One indivisible pipeline producing one model: build → data → train → single training_output.txt and single cifar10_quick_iter_500.caffemodel. No step can be worked in parallel with another; there is no fan-out across files, cases or targets.
evidence.B8: The instruction pins nearly everything — repo (BVLC Caffe 1.0.0), path (/app/caffe), CPU-only build, exact iteration count, solver path examples/cifar10/cifar10_quick_solver.prototxt, log path /app/caffe/training_output.txt, model name cifar10_quick_iter_{n}.caffemodel. The residual gap is content the agent derives: the log's contents and the accuracy figures. A shortcut (pip-installed caffe, a truncated log, or an accuracy line copied rather than produced) would still look well-formed against every stated constraint.
evidence.C2: Consistent with B3=2: a source build of Caffe plus dataset conversion plus a training run occupies most of the 3600s agent budget. Mandatory per-step stops are material but do not dominate work measured in compile minutes and training epochs.
evidence.C4: The instruction states the procedure in outline — clone this repo, build CPU-only, use this solver, run 500 iterations — and the method is the conventional documented Caffe CIFAR-10 flow (get_cifar10.sh / create_cifar10.sh / train_quick.sh). Nothing leads with a symptom, and no supplied dataset or codebase must be inspected before the approach can be chosen; only build-toolchain and dependency-version choices are open.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/plan-and-execute.js composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gates: the make build exiting 0, existence of examples/cifar10/cifar10_quick_iter_500.caffemodel, and a parse of /app/caffe/training_output.txt asserting test accuracy > 0.45 and train − test ≤ 0.05)

A second, likelier shortcut: with the CPU_ONLY flag left unset in Makefile.config the build fails against CUDA, and the agent pivots to a pip wheel or a substitute framework, producing outputs at the right paths that were never made by BVLC Caffe 1.0.0.

B5 is unusually strong for this corpus because the acceptance figures — test accuracy above 45%, within 5% of train — are readable from the log the agent itself is told to write, giving a real iterate-until-target loop rather than a hidden-verifier surprise. Costs are low: the method is the documented Caffe CIFAR-10 flow rather than a diagnosis (C4=1), and orchestration overhead is small against a source compile plus a training run (C2=1). B8 is only 1 — the output contract is pinned down to paths and filenames, so difficulty here is not drift risk. Net_live lands clearly positive, driven by B1 with B5 close behind.

rows.name: cancel-async-tasks

evidence.B1: The instruction states one deliverable with two layered requirements: "max_concurrent is the max number of tasks that can be run concurrently" and then "Sometimes I cancel runs via keyboard interrupt but I want the tasks' cleanup code to still run." A natural order exists (get the concurrency runner working, then make it cancellation-safe), but no step consumes an artifact or derived value produced by an earlier step, and reversing the order does not silently corrupt the result.
evidence.B3: metadata: expertMinutes 120, at the top of the profile's ~30-120 minute band; agentTimeoutSec 900 (15 minutes), far below the 7200 threshold that would justify 2. The deliverable is a single file, /app/run.py, with one function.
evidence.B5: The agent can verify itself: it can write async jobs with try/finally cleanup markers, run them under run_tasks, and send a keyboard interrupt to check that "the tasks' cleanup code to still run" — a pass/fail check with a worked shape but no quantity to improve. Nothing in the instruction gives a number, rate, or baseline to move toward; max_concurrent is a caller-supplied parameter, not a target the agent optimizes.
evidence.B6: "Put the function in a file called /app/run.py so that it can be imported using from run import run_tasks" — one function in one file. There are no independent units that could be fanned out and verified separately.
evidence.B8: Path, import form and signature are pinned ("async run_tasks(tasks: list[Callable[[], Awaitable[None]]], max_concurrent: int) -> None"), which caps drift, but the central requirement is stated purely in outcome terms: "I want the tasks' cleanup code to still run" on keyboard interrupt. Nothing specifies whether cleanup must complete before the interrupt propagates, whether the exception is re-raised, or how pending-but-unstarted tasks are handled — two competent agents would plausibly ship materially different semantics that both read as satisfying the sentence.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 120 and agentTimeoutSec 900 put this in the profile's ~30-120 minute band: a single-file, single-function deliverable where per-step mandatory stops are a noticeable fraction of the total work.
evidence.C4: The instruction leads with a construction request ("Create a Python function called async run_tasks..."), not a symptom or complaint, and names no supplied dataset, log, or existing codebase to inspect first — "Just use the system python to implement. Feel free to install packages if you need to." The method is conventional for the stated domain (bounded-concurrency asyncio) with the cancellation mechanism the only open choice.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/tdd.js
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent writes the obvious asyncio.Semaphore + gather implementation, confirms max_concurrent is respected on a happy-path script, and declares done — never exercising the interrupt path, because simulating SIGINT against its own event loop is awkward and the instruction mentions it only in a trailing sentence. The shipped run.py then lets KeyboardInterrupt tear the loop down while cancelled coroutines' finally blocks are still awaiting, so cleanup is silently skipped for in-flight tasks while the artifact looks complete and passes every check the agent bothered to run.
rows.rationale: Small, exactly-addressed deliverable — one function, one file, one import path — over a 120-expert-minute, 900-second-timeout budget, so horizon and decomposability contribute almost nothing and C2 lands squarely in the ceremony-is-noticeable band. The one real benefit signal is B8: the cancellation requirement is stated as an outcome (\"I want the tasks' cleanup code to still run\") with none of its semantics pinned, so a confident, well-formed, wrong implementation is the likely vanilla outcome and that is a nameable concrete failure rather than vague unease. B1 is a weak 1 — the two requirements have a natural sequence but no dependency that silently corrupts anything if reordered — and B5 is 1 because the agent can self-check whether cleanup ran but has no quantity to improve. C4 stays at 1: the instruction is a construction request in a conventional domain with no supplied input to inspect first, and specifying the output file does not raise it. Cost is driven by C2 against a modest-sized task; the honest read is a mildly negative net_live, well short of any strong routing signal in either direction.

Note that B2 is pinned at 3 corpus-wide, so the presence of a verifier is not evidence here.

rows.name: db-wal-recovery

evidence.B1: The instruction states an explicit numbered chain: "1. Fix the WAL file so SQLite can read it 2. Extract ALL data from the database (including WAL changes) 3. Create a JSON file in /app/recovered.json". The repair produces the state the extraction consumes, and the extraction produces the content the JSON write consumes. Violating the order does not error — it silently yields a plausible answer, as the instruction itself warns: "SQLite may only show the base data (5 records) instead of all 11 records that should be there."
evidence.B3: metadata expertMinutes=45, difficulty=medium, agentTimeoutSec=900 (15 min) — well inside the ~30–120 minute band and far below the corpus median of 120 expert-minutes.
evidence.B5: "You should recover all 11 records total" gives the agent a quantity it can compute for itself (rows in recovered.json) and a stated figure to reach, so it can tell whether an attempt at the WAL repair improved things (5 → 11). It is short of 3 because the substance the verifier actually checks — the per-record values, "{\"id\": 1, \"name\": \"item1\", \"value\": X}" — cannot be scored by the agent at all; only the count is measurable.
evidence.B6: A single deliverable, "a JSON file in /app/recovered.json", produced from one database in /app/. There are no independent units to fan out; the three listed steps are strictly sequential on the same artifact.
evidence.B8: The output contract is pinned — exact path /app/recovered.json, exact shape "[{\"id\": 1, \"name\": \"item1\", \"value\": X}, ...]", "sorted by id", and a fixed cardinality of 11. The only unpinned part is the recovered values themselves, so a bad recovery (or invented records) would still be well-formed and would read as complete. Format pinned, content derived → 1.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes=45 and agentTimeoutSec=900 put this in the ~30–120 minute band; per-step mandatory stops are a noticeable fraction of a task whose whole body of work is repair-one-file, query, dump JSON.
evidence.C4: The instruction leads with a symptom, not a procedure: "the WAL file appears to be corrupted or encrypted" — the agent is not even told which it is (tags list both "encryption" and "recovery"). The first real step is diagnosing the WAL header/frame damage or the encryption scheme; naming the output file /app/recovered.json does not reduce this.

rows.processRecommendation: custom
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent opens the database with `sqlite3` (or a Python sqlite3 connection), sees the 5 base rows, dumps them — or pads the file out to 11 plausible-looking synthetic records to satisfy the stated count — and writes a perfectly well-formed /app/recovered.json without ever repairing the WAL. The artifact validates against every visible constraint in the instruction (path, key names, sorted by id) while the `value` fields are silently wrong, and the agent declares success.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is C4=3: the instruction opens with a symptom ("corrupted or encrypted") rather than a method, so the shape of the fix is discovered by inspecting the WAL, and any process encoded up front would be guessing at the repair technique. Against that, the real benefit signal is B1=3 — an explicit fix→extract→emit chain whose violation yields a well-formed JSON with the wrong 5 records, which is exactly the concrete vanilla failure named above. But the task is small (45 expert-minutes, 15-minute agent timeout, one output file), so B3=1, B6=0, and C2=2 all push the other way, and the exact output contract holds drift risk to 1. Benefit is genuine but narrow and concentrated in ordering; cost is dominated by diagnosis-first uncertainty on a task too short to amortize orchestration.

rows.name: distribution-search

evidence.B1: The instruction lists numbered items but they are not a dependency chain: "1. Find a probability distribution with the following exact properties... 2. Save the results in the exact file: /app/dist.npy". There is a natural reading order (derive/solve the parameters, then serialize the array), but no earlier artifact is consumed by a later phase in a way that silently corrupts the result if reordered — the whole thing is one solve followed by one write.
evidence.B3: metadata: "expertMinutes": 120 and "agentTimeoutSec": 3600 — one hour of agent wall-clock, at the top of the profile's ~30–120 minute band. One script, one output file; no phase produces an artifact a later sitting must resume from.
evidence.B5: The agent can compute both objectives itself from the formulas given in the instruction ("KL(P||U) = Σ P(i) * log(P(i) / U(i))", "KL(U||P) = Σ U(i) * log(U(i) / P(i))") and compare against a stated finish line: "forward KL divergence KL(P||U) is 10.0", "backward KL divergence KL(U||P) is 10.0", "the tolerance for both KL divergences is 0.001 (i.e., |KL - 10.0| ≤ 0.001)". This is a scored iterate-until-target loop with a defined target, entirely evaluable before the verifier runs.
evidence.B6: One indivisible artifact: a single array of length 150,000 written to "/app/dist.npy". The two KL constraints are coupled on the same vector and cannot be solved as independent units; there is no N-files/N-cases fan-out.
evidence.B8: Path, type and validity are pinned — "/app/dist.npy: NumPy array of probability distribution", "vocabulary size is 150,000", "The distribution should be a valid probability distribution" — so the shape of a wrong answer is constrained. Residual risk is only that a derived array is off-target (e.g. KL within 0.01 rather than 0.001, or containing zeros making backward KL infinite) while still looking like a well-formed 150,000-entry distribution.
evidence.C2: "expertMinutes": 120 puts this at the top of the profile's ~30–120 minute band; the deliverable is a single Python script producing one .npy file, so mandatory per-step stops and journaling are a noticeable fraction of the total work.
evidence.C4: The instruction leads with the method, not a symptom: it gives both KL formulas explicitly, fixes the vocabulary size and tolerance, and names the toolchain ("We provide numpy and scipy to help with the calculations."). No supplied dataset, log or existing codebase must be inspected before the approach can be chosen — what is open is the numerical parametrization/solver choice within a conventional constrained-optimization approach.

rows.processRecommendation: library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (paired with an iterative-convergence loop on |KL - 10.0| ≤ 0.001 for both directions)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: A vanilla agent picks a two-level (spike + tail) family, tunes it until forward KL(P||U) lands on 10.0, and saves /app/dist.npy after checking only that one number — leaving backward KL(U||P) far from 10.0 (or effectively infinite because tail masses underflowed to 0), and declares success. The silently-wrong artifact is well-formed: a length-150,000 nonnegative array summing to 1, so nothing looks broken until the hidden verifier recomputes the second divergence and the sum-to-one/positivity check under float64.
rows.rationale: The one dimension that genuinely favors enforcement here is B5: the instruction hands the agent both KL formulas, an exact target of 10.0, and a tolerance of 0.001, so a scored convergence loop with a real finish line is available and a gate would be a shell exit code rather than self-assertion. Everything else is thin — a single 150,000-entry array in one file (B6=0), an exactly pinned output contract that leaves little room for a plausible-but-different artifact (B8=1), and a 120-expert-minute / 3600-second horizon that fits one sitting (B3=1). Cost pushes back: at ~2 hours of work the per-step ceremony is a visible fraction of the task (C2=2), while the method is stated well enough that only the solver parametrization is open (C4=1). The concrete vanilla failure — optimizing one divergence, never re-checking the other or the underflow-to-zero tail, and shipping a well-formed but out-of-tolerance array — is real but is exactly what a single self-run verification script catches, so the benefit is concentrated in one dimension rather than spread across the live set.

rows.name: dna-assembly

evidence.B1: The instruction gives four fragments plus a target: "input, egfp, flag, and snap ... combine them to make the output plasmid." Fragment order/orientation and junction positions must first be derived by comparing the parts against the "desired circular output plasmid", and those derived junctions then determine the 4-nt fusion overhangs, which in turn determine each primer's 5' tail ("I don't have enzyme cut-sites in my sequences so I'll need to PCR amplify them first"; "check that the enzyme cut-sites you design satisfy NEB's requirements"). One step's output is consumed by the next, and the wrong order yields a well-formed but non-assembling primer set. Not 3: no explicit multi-phase ordering is stated, and the Tm/length rules are checks rather than further chained derivations.
evidence.B3: metadata: expertMinutes 60, agentTimeoutSec 1800 (30 min). Squarely in the profile's ~30-120 minute band; a single sitting producing one small output file, primers.fasta.
evidence.B5: The agent can measure and iterate on its own: "The output of primer3's oligotm tool should be considered the ground truth for melting temperatures with the following flags: `-tp 1 -sc 1 -mv 50 -dv 2 -n 0.8 -d 500`", with stated finish lines - "melting temperature between 58 and 72 degrees celsius", "at most 5 degrees celsius apart", annealing region "between 15 and 45 nucleotides". Extend/trim the annealing region, re-run oligotm, and see whether it moved toward target: a computable quantity plus explicit figures to hit.
evidence.B6: Four templates each needing a fwd/rev pair ("TEMPLATENAME can be one of input, egfp, flag, or snap, and DIR can be either fwd OR rev") gives some per-template fan-out, but the fragments are coupled: adjacent fragments must share complementary overhangs for a "one-pot golden gate assembly" and the overhang set must be mutually compatible, so the eight primers cannot be designed independently. One indivisible deliverable file.
evidence.B8: Output is pinned tightly: "The output fasta file should be titled primers.fasta", header format "`>TEMPLATENAME_DIR`", fixed template names and directions, "should not have any blank lines", plus numeric bounds on length and Tm and "Output the minimum number of primer pairs necessary". Format and file are fully determined; only the nucleotide content is derived, so an incorrect design would still look well-formed. The long constraint list narrows rather than widens the space.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 60 with agentTimeoutSec 1800 - the ~30-120 minute band, where mandatory per-step stops are a noticeable fraction of a job whose deliverable is a single eight-record FASTA file.
evidence.C4: The method is conventional for the stated domain and the instruction fixes the tooling: NEBridge Golden Gate with BsaI-HF v2, PCR tails carrying cut-sites, and "primer3's oligotm" as Tm ground truth with exact flags. Nothing leads with a symptom or complaint, and the procedure (locate junctions in the given output plasmid, append BsaI site + spacer + overhang, tune annealing length into the Tm window) is knowable before opening sequences.fasta; inspecting the file supplies parameter values, not the plan.

rows.processRecommendation: custom
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent designs plausible BsaI-tailed primers and computes melting temperatures with a convenient library (Biopython Tm_NN or a rule-of-thumb 2/4 formula) instead of running `oligotm -tp 1 -sc 1 -mv 50 -dv 2 -n 0.8 -d 500` on the annealing region alone, then writes primers.fasta and declares success; the file is perfectly well-formed and header-correct while several pairs sit outside 58-72 C or more than 5 C apart. The sibling failure is skipping the explicit "check that the enzyme cut-sites you design satisfy NEB's requirements" step - omitting the 5' spacer bases BsaI needs to cut efficiently, or choosing overhangs that are palindromic or duplicated between junctions - which silently breaks the one-pot assembly while every stated formatting rule still passes.
rows.rationale: B5 dominates the benefit side: the instruction hands the agent its own oracle - oligotm with exact flags, a 58-72 C window, a 5 C pair-delta, and a 15-45 nt length band - so an iterate-and-measure loop with a defined finish line exists before any hidden test runs, which is exactly what a convergence gate enforces. B1=2 adds a genuine derivation chain (junctions from the target plasmid, then overhangs, then primer tails), and the vanilla failure is concrete: substituting a convenient Tm estimate for the mandated tool, or skipping the NEB cut-site check, both produce a file that looks entirely correct. Against that, the task is one 60-minute deliverable - a single eight-record FASTA - so C2=2 charges real ceremony overhead, and C4 is low because the kit, enzyme, and Tm tool are all named, leaving no method to discover. B8 stays at 1 despite the "hard" difficulty label: path, header format, template names, and the blank-line rule are all pinned, so drift has little room. Net lands just on the enforcement-positive side, driven by the measurable convergence loop rather than by difficulty.

rows.name: dna-insert

evidence.B1: Steps chain: the input and output plasmid sequences in sequences.fasta must first be compared to locate the edit, which determines where the annealing arms start; only then is the annealing-only region defined, and only then can Tm be computed -- 'Melting temperature should be computed with respect to only the part of the primers that anneal to the input template.' Computing Tm before fixing the annealing/tail split silently yields wrong values, so a later step consumes an earlier step's derived value.
evidence.B3: Metadata: expertMinutes 30, difficulty 'medium', agentTimeoutSec 1800 -- the shortest tier, far below the 7200 threshold and well under the corpus median of 120 expert-minutes; a focused single sitting.
evidence.B5: Stated figures plus the measuring instrument are handed over: 'length between 15 and 45 nucleotides', 'melting temperature between 58 and 72 degrees celsius', pair Tm 'at most 5 degrees celsius apart', and the instruction names primer3's oligotm with exact flags (-tp 1 -sc 1 -mv 50 -dv 2 -n 0.8 -d 500) as ground truth. The agent can score candidates itself and iterate until every figure is met, with 'Output the minimum number of primer pairs necessary' as a defined finish line.
evidence.B6: One indivisible deliverable -- 'The output fasta file should be titled primers.fasta.' The primers are mutually constrained (pair Tm within 5 degrees, minimum number of pairs), so there are no independent units to fan out.
evidence.B8: Path, format and ordering are pinned -- 'grouped by primer pairs in the output fasta file with the forward primer being listed first' -- and the numeric rules narrow the space further; but the nucleotide sequences are agent-derived, so a mis-chosen annealing arm still yields a well-formed FASTA that reads as correct.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 30 and agentTimeoutSec 1800 put this in the under-30-minutes band: a handful of oligotm invocations and one small FASTA. Per-step mandatory stops and journaling would cost more than the work itself. Scored as the mirror of B3=0.
evidence.C4: No symptom or complaint is presented, but the method cannot be fixed until the supplied input is inspected: 'The file titled sequences.fasta contains the sequence for a circular input plasmid, and a desired output plasmid.' Whether the edit is an insertion, deletion or substitution, its size, and hence whether one primer pair can carry it or 'the minimum number of primer pairs necessary' is greater than one, is only knowable after diffing the two sequences. Q5 SDM primer design itself is conventional for the domain, so this stops at the inspect-a-supplied-input line rather than the diagnosis line.

rows.processRecommendation: custom
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent computes melting temperature over the whole primer including the 5-prime insertion tail -- or with Biopython / an ad-hoc nearest-neighbour formula instead of oligotm with the specified flags -- and writes a perfectly well-formed primers.fasta whose annealing regions fall outside 58-72 C or more than 5 C apart, declaring success without ever running the specified ground-truth tool on the annealing-only substring.
rows.rationale: A 30-expert-minute, single-artifact task whose cost side dominates: C2=3 because per-step orchestration stops would exceed the work, and C4=2 because the primer strategy is only determinable after diffing the two plasmid sequences in the supplied FASTA. The one real benefit is B5=3 -- the instruction names oligotm with exact flags as ground truth and gives numeric Tm and length windows, so the agent has a genuine self-scored loop with a finish line, which is exactly the loop a vanilla agent tends to skip. B1=2 reflects the real dependency (locate the edit, fix the annealing/tail boundary, then measure Tm on the annealing part only), but B3=0, B6=0 and B8=1 leave little else: the output contract is pinned tightly enough that a wrong answer is checkable. The counterfactual is concrete -- Tm measured over the wrong substring or with the wrong tool -- but enforcing that single check does not need a journal, breakpoints, or a resumable run.

rows.name: extract-elf

evidence.B1: "extract memory values from the binary and output them as a JSON object with memory addresses as keys" — inside the single extract.js the values are chained: the header must be parsed to locate the program/section header table, that table's offsets and virtual addresses must then be read, and only then can file offsets be converted into the address keys shown in the example ("4194304", "4194308"). Getting that sequence wrong yields a plausible but wrongly-keyed object. One deliverable, but a real intra-file dependency chain; no explicit multi-stage first-X-then-Y is stated, so not 3.
evidence.B3: metadata `expertMinutes: 30` and `agentTimeoutSec: 900` (15 minutes) — the shortest tier in this corpus, far below the 120-minute corpus median. One focused sitting; nothing in the instruction produces an artifact a later phase consumes.
evidence.B5: "For any address you include in your output, the value MUST match the reference solution" plus the worked example `{"4194304": 1784774249, ...}` give the agent a pass/fail self-check (compare its parse against readelf/objdump output, or against the two example words). The second criterion, "at least 75% of the memory values that are present in the reference solution", is a figure the agent cannot evaluate — the denominator is the hidden reference — so there is no scale to iterate against.
evidence.B6: A single deliverable: "Write me a program extract.js", invoked as one command `node extract.js /app/a.out > out.json`. No independent units to fan out.
evidence.B8: Path, invocation and format are pinned exactly — "extract.js", "node extract.js /app/a.out > out.json", "Example output format: {\"4194304\": 1784774249, ...}", "values should be integers, not strings" — so the artifact's shape is determined. What remains agent-derived is which addresses to include (which segments, what stride, whether zero-filled regions count); the 75% coverage clause concedes that set varies, so an under- or over-inclusive extraction would still look well-formed. Format pinned, content derived.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 30` with `agentTimeoutSec: 900` — a single-script task at the bottom of the corpus range. Mandatory stops after every step, a journal and gate turns would cost more wall-clock and tokens than writing the parser itself. Scored as the mirror of B3=0.
evidence.C4: The instruction does not lead with a symptom, so not 3; but the method cannot be chosen until the supplied input is inspected: "I have provided a file a.out that's a compiled C binary" — the agent must examine a.out to learn its format (ELF class, endianness, which segments hold the initialized data, what "memory values" means at addresses like 4194304) before it can decide what the parser does. The named output file does not settle this.

rows.processRecommendation: custom
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent parses only the first PT_LOAD segment (or only .text/.data) and emits a well-formed JSON object whose keys look right, but with a wrong word stride or wrong endianness — every value is confidently incorrect, which fails criterion 1 outright — and it declares success on the basis that the file it produced is valid JSON, never cross-checking its extracted words against `readelf`/`objdump` output or against the two example values it was handed.
rows.rationale: Cost dominates: a 30-expert-minute, 900-second single-script task (C2=3) whose method still requires inspecting the supplied binary first (C4=2) leaves almost nothing for orchestration to buy. The benefit side is thin — one file, one sitting, no fan-out, and a format pinned tightly enough by the worked example that a wrong answer is mostly a wrong-values answer rather than a wrong-artifact answer. B1=2 is the only real signal: ELF parsing has a genuine intra-file dependency chain (header to header table to segment offsets to address keys) that produces plausible-but-wrong output when taken out of order. The counterfactual is concrete — a partial or mis-strided extraction that is valid JSON and silently fails criterion 1 — but that is a defect an ordinary session catches by diffing against readelf, not one that needs a mandatory stop after every step.

rows.name: extract-moves-from-video

evidence.B1: "Transcribe the entire contents of the text, and create a file /app/solution.txt that has all the moves they input" — the move list is derived from the transcription, which is derived from frames sampled out of /app/video.mp4. Each stage consumes the previous stage's intermediate artifact, so extracting moves before a complete, deduplicated transcript exists silently yields a wrong list.
evidence.B3: metadata: expertMinutes 120, agentTimeoutSec 1800 (well under the 7200 threshold for a 2). Top of the ~30-120 minute band; one long sitting, no resume expected.
evidence.B5: "one per line, in the format 'n' or 'get bag' etc." gives a worked example of the expected shape, and the game's own on-screen responses let the agent sanity-check that a transcribed command is plausible. That is a pass/fail check with no scale; no target figure or baseline is stated.
evidence.B6: A single deliverable — one file, /app/solution.txt, whose lines must be in play order. Frame batches could nominally be OCR'd in parallel, but the instruction describes one indivisible artifact, not N independently verifiable units.
evidence.B8: The output contract is pinned — exact path /app/solution.txt, one move per line, format exemplified ('n', 'get bag'). Drift is bounded to content: an OCR misread or a dropped stretch of video produces a well-formed list that reads as complete, but the deliverable's shape cannot wander.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 120 with agentTimeoutSec 1800 — squarely in the ~30-120 minute band where mandatory per-step stops are a noticeable fraction of the total work.
evidence.C4: The instruction names the input ("A video ... located at /app/video.mp4") and the output but no method. Frame rate, resolution, whether the terminal text scrolls, and whether OCR is even needed are unknowable until the supplied video is inspected — the procedure cannot be chosen before looking at the input. The instruction does not lead with a symptom, so the diagnosis line does not fire.

rows.processRecommendation: custom
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent samples frames at too coarse an interval (or stops after the first few minutes of the video), OCRs what it has, and writes a syntactically perfect /app/solution.txt missing moves from the middle or tail of the playthrough — a plausible, well-formed list it declares complete without ever checking transcript coverage against the video's full duration. The sibling failure is not deduplicating consecutive frames showing the same screen, emitting repeated moves that also look valid.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is C4=2 paired with a middling horizon: the extraction method genuinely cannot be fixed before the agent has looked at /app/video.mp4, so any process encoded up front is a guess about frame sampling and OCR strategy, and at 120 expert-minutes the per-step stops are a visible fraction of the work. On the benefit side only B1 rises above 1 — frames feed a transcript which feeds the move list, a real chain where working out of order silently corrupts the output. B8 stays low because the instruction pins path, one-move-per-line format, and gives literal examples, so drift is confined to content accuracy rather than deliverable shape; difficulty here is not latitude. B5 and B6 earn 1 each: a worked format example plus in-video game responses give a pass/fail check with no scale, and the task is one indivisible file. The counterfactual is concrete — incomplete video coverage yielding a well-formed but truncated move list — so no cap applies.

rows.name: feal-differential-cryptanalysis

evidence.B1: "Implement a chosen plaintext attack that recovers the value of key[5]" against "/app/feal.py [which] implements a FEAL-like encryption function" — the differential characteristic must be derived from the actual round function in feal.py before chosen-plaintext pairs can be generated, and those pairs' ciphertexts are what the key[5] candidate scoring consumes. Intermediate values inside one file, consumed in sequence: derive characteristic -> generate pairs -> filter/score candidates. Reversing or guessing the characteristic yields a recovery routine that returns a plausible-but-wrong uint32.
evidence.B3: metadata expertMinutes: 480 and difficulty: "hard" place this at the top of the 2-8 hour band and far above the corpus median of 120. agentTimeoutSec is 1800, below the 7200 marker for a 3.
evidence.B5: The agent holds the cipher source (/app/feal.py) and the hint that "Each of the 6 round keys is derived from a 16 bit seed", so it can instantiate keys itself and check recovered key[5] against ground truth, measuring success rate over many random seeds. Plus a stated finish line to beat: "Your attack should run in less than 30 seconds." Both a computable quantity and a target figure.
evidence.B6: One deliverable, one entry point: "implemented in /app/attack.py, and should implement a function called attack(encrypt_fn)" returning a single value. No independent units to fan out.
evidence.B8: Output contract is pinned — file path /app/attack.py, function name attack(encrypt_fn), return type "the uint32 value of key[5]" — so the shape of a wrong answer is constrained. Residual gap: the recovery logic is entirely agent-derived, so an attack that works on the one seed the agent tried still returns a well-formed uint32 and looks complete.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes: 480 sits in the ~2-8 hour band; per-step orchestration stops are material but do not dominate a task of this size (consistent with B3=2).
evidence.C4: The instruction names a supplied input that must be read before the method can be fixed: "The file /app/feal.py implements a FEAL-like encryption function" — FEAL-like, not FEAL, so round count, F-function and key schedule are unknown until inspected, and the choice of differential characteristic depends on them. Not a 3: the instruction states the procedure class ("chosen plaintext attack", "differential attack") rather than leading with a symptom.

rows.processRecommendation: custom
rows.vanillaFailureMode: A vanilla session validates the attack against a single hardcoded key seed it generated itself, sees key[5] come back correct, and declares done — shipping a routine that depends on that seed's structure (or that quietly brute-forces the 16-bit seed against one known pair rather than doing the differential recovery) and then fails the verifier on other keys or blows the stated 30-second budget. The skipped step is the multi-seed success-rate and timing check, which nothing in the instruction forces the agent to run before stopping.
rows.rationale: Decisive factor is the combination of a long horizon (480 expert-minutes, hardest band in this corpus) with a genuinely self-measurable target — the agent can instantiate keys from the disclosed 16-bit seed space, check recovered key[5] against truth across many seeds, and time itself against the stated 30-second limit — which is exactly the loop convergence enforcement is for. Ordering is real but internal to one file: the characteristic derived from feal.py feeds pair generation feeds candidate scoring, so a wrong sequence yields a plausible wrong uint32. Against that, the deliverable is a single indivisible function with a fully pinned signature and return type, so decomposability is nil and drift risk is low — difficulty here is not drift. Cost is moderate: the method cannot be chosen until the FEAL-like variant in /app/feal.py is read (C4=2), but at this task size orchestration overhead is not dominant (C2=1). The counterfactual is concrete, not vague: premature success on a single tested seed.

rows.name: feal-linear-cryptanalysis

evidence.B1: "Implement a known-plaintext attack that recovers the key of the cipher. Prove you have recovered the key by decrypting all the ciphertexts in the file /app/ciphertexts.txt, and saving your answer in the file /app/plaintexts.txt" — chained dependencies: read /app/feal.c to derive the cipher structure, then build a linear approximation, then recover round keys from /app/pairs.txt (with "Each of the 4 round keys is derived from a 20 bit seed", later rounds' recovery consumes the earlier recovered subkeys), then feed the recovered key into decryption to produce plaintexts.txt. Each stage consumes the prior stage's derived value, and the wrong order silently yields plausible-but-wrong plaintexts.
evidence.B3: metadata expertMinutes: 960 (16 hours), difficulty "hard" — above the ~8-hour line in the profile ladder and far above the corpus median of 120.
evidence.B5: "the file /app/pairs.txt contain 32 plaintext-ciphertext pairs" plus /app/feal.c and /app/decrypt.c give the agent a self-computable quantity: how many of the 32 known pairs a candidate key reproduces, and per-candidate bias counts from the linear approximation. The agent can tell whether a key guess improved without the hidden verifier, but no target figure is stated.
evidence.B6: "Each of the 4 round keys is derived from a 20 bit seed" — the four round-key recoveries are nominally separate units but are sequentially dependent (peeling rounds) and produce one indivisible deliverable, /app/plaintexts.txt. No genuine fan-out.
evidence.B8: Output is pinned by path and derivation: "saving your answer in the file /app/plaintexts.txt", produced by decrypting "all the ciphertexts in the file /app/ciphertexts.txt". Content is derived by the agent from a recovered key, so a bad key still yields a well-formed file of wrong plaintexts; the exact line/encoding format is not stated. Scope is otherwise bounded to a handful of named files.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes: 960 — well over the ~8-hour anchor, so mandatory per-step stops are a rounding error against the work.
evidence.C4: The instruction names the family of method ("a linear attack that recovers round-keys") but not the procedure: the usable linear characteristic can only be chosen after inspecting the supplied "/app/feal.c implements a FEAL-like encryption function" and "/app/decrypt.c" — supplied inputs named in the instruction that must be reverse-engineered before the attack's shape is known. No symptom-led diagnosis, so not 3.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/plan-and-execute.js composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gate: the candidate key must re-encrypt all 32 pairs in /app/pairs.txt before plaintexts.txt is written)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent burns the session on partial round-key recovery, gets a candidate seed that reproduces some but not all of the 32 pairs in /app/pairs.txt, skips the round-trip check against those pairs, and writes a fully well-formed /app/plaintexts.txt of garbage decryptions — or falls back to brute-forcing only the first round key and declares success because a file now exists at the required path.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is horizon: 960 expert-minutes with a strictly chained derivation (understand feal.c → build the linear approximation → recover the 4 round keys in order → decrypt and emit plaintexts.txt), which drives B3=3 and B1=3 while making orchestration overhead negligible (C2=0). The task also supplies its own scoring signal — 32 known pairs a candidate key can be checked against — so a gate on "the recovered key reproduces all 32 pairs" is a real shell-checkable condition rather than agent self-assertion, giving B5=2. Working against that, C4=2: the attack's shape cannot be fixed until /app/feal.c has been reverse-engineered, so any pre-encoded characteristic-derivation step would be a guess. Drift risk is low (B8=1) because the output path and its derivation are pinned — difficulty here is not drift — and decomposability is minimal (B6=1) since the round-key recoveries depend on one another sequentially. Net_live lands clearly positive, driven by horizon and ordering rather than by the task merely being hard.

rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent greps bottle.py, latches onto the first plausible-looking weakness (e.g. path traversal in `static_file` or header handling), writes report.jsonl with that CWE id in the correct format, makes a cosmetic edit, and declares success without ever running `pytest -rA` — or runs it, sees failures, and rationalizes them as pre-existing. rows.processRecommendation: custom
rows.vanillaFailureMode: A vanilla agent finds the first plausible candidate — say a stash entry or one branch — merges it into master, and declares success while a second source of the lost work (a dangling commit from an amended/reset HEAD, or a detached-HEAD commit still in the reflog) is never recovered, so master silently ends up with only part of the changes. The instruction opens with a symptom ("now I can't find those changes") and no procedure, which is the top line of the C4 ladder at 3, and at 5 expert minutes with a 900-second agent timeout C2 is also 3 — together those pin Cost_live at the ceiling. rows.name: fix-ocaml-gc

rows.vanillaFailureMode: Unable to localize the corruption in the run-length-compressed free list within one context window of slow bootstrap cycles, the agent takes the cheap exit: it reverts or disables the run-length compression (or patches around the crash site in the collector) until `make -C testsuite one DIR=tests/basic` goes green, then declares done — the stated sweeping improvement is silently gone and the real invariant violation is never found. The secondary failure is stopping after a partial build that no longer segfaults and claiming success without ever completing the full bootstrap and running the suite.

The instruction states no procedure and does not lead with a symptom.

Step 2 destroys the unreachable object step 1 must read, so purging (or gc --prune) first silently makes the correct answer unrecoverable — one step consumes what an earlier step produced.

rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent reads requirement 2 ("clean up the secret ... cannot be found anywhere") and runs the purge first — filter-repo/filter-branch plus `reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now` — deleting the unreachable commit holding the secret before extracting it. /app/secret.txt then gets an empty or guessed value while the repo looks clean, so the agent declares success on a task it has made unrecoverable. Everything else sits at or near the floor — a 30-expert-minute task with a 900s agent timeout, one repo, one indivisible chain of steps, and an exactly pinned output path and value. Cost dominates: C2=3 because per-step stops exceed the work itself, and C4=2 because the recovery route is unknowable until the repo's reflog and object store are inspected. rows.name: git-multibranch

evidence.B1: The pieces feed each other: a bare repo must exist at `git@localhost:/git/project` before the `post-receive` hook can be installed in it; the hook's checkout destinations are exactly the document roots Nginx must serve (`https://localhost:8443/index.html` and `.../dev/index.html`); and the self-signed certificate must exist before the Nginx TLS server block will load. Writing the hook's output paths against the wrong Nginx root yields a server that starts cleanly but serves the wrong or missing content — a downstream step consuming an earlier step's artifact. Not a strict first-X-then-Y-then-Z chain, since several components can be configured in either order as long as they agree.
evidence.B3: `expertMinutes: 180` (3 hours) sits in the profile's ~2-8 hour band; `difficulty: medium`, `category: system-administration`, spanning sshd password auth, a bare git repo, a post-receive hook, self-signed TLS and Nginx. (`agentTimeoutSec: 900` is below the 7200 marker, so no upward push.)
evidence.B5: The instruction hands the agent the entire acceptance procedure — "Cloning the repository... Creating a main branch... Pushing both branches... Verifying that https://localhost:8443/index.html returns 'main branch content'" — so the agent can rerun it locally and know whether it is right, and it states one measurable quantity with a finish line: "The deployment should complete within 3 seconds of the push." Timing is a number the agent can compute and improve; the rest of the loop is pass/fail.
evidence.B6: Nominally separable sub-systems (SSH access, git repo + hook, TLS cert, Nginx vhost) but they compose into one end-to-end path that is only verifiable as a whole: a push must reach two endpoints. The two branches are not independent units — both are produced by the same single `post-receive` hook.
evidence.B8: The output contract is pinned: exact SSH URL `git@localhost:/git/project`, exact password "password", exact URLs and exact expected bodies ("main branch content", "dev branch content"), plus a named hook type and a 3-second budget. Implementation details (docroot layout, sshd config, cert parameters) are the agent's, so a mistake there would still look well-formed, but a wrong result is visibly wrong at the stated URLs.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 180` falls in the profile's ~2-8 hour band; per-step mandatory stops are material but do not dominate three hours of multi-service configuration.
evidence.C4: No symptom or complaint to diagnose and no supplied dataset/codebase to inspect first — the instruction states the target architecture directly ("Set up a Git server... over SSH", "deploy contents from two branches... using Nginx", "Each push... should trigger a deployment via a `post-receive` hook"). The method is conventional sysadmin practice; only tooling and config-layout choices (sshd variant, docroot arrangement, cert generation) are open.

rows.processRecommendation: library/specializations/devops-sre-platform/ composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gate = the instruction's own clone/push/curl sequence)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent configures sshd, Nginx and a `post-receive` hook, hand-places an `index.html` in the docroot, curls `https://localhost:8443/index.html` successfully, and declares done — never performing the stated end-to-end clone→push→verify cycle. The hook then fails silently in the real push path (sshd's minimal environment lacks git on PATH, or `GIT_DIR` is inherited so the `--work-tree` checkout lands in the wrong place), or the dev-branch checkout is written over the main docroot instead of the `dev/` subpath, so `https://localhost:8443/dev/index.html` 404s or returns "main branch content".
rows.rationale: Benefit is carried by the integration coupling (B1=2: the hook's checkout targets must match the Nginx roots, and the cert must precede the TLS vhost) and by a 3-hour expert estimate (B3=2), while cost stays low because the instruction states the architecture outright rather than opening with a symptom (C4=1) and three hours absorbs orchestration overhead (C2=1). The counterfactual is concrete and typical of this task family: the agent verifies a hand-placed file rather than the real push path, so a hook that is broken only under sshd's environment ships as green. Drift risk is genuinely low (B8=1) — the URLs, the exact response bodies and the SSH endpoint are all pinned, so a wrong answer is visibly wrong; the freedom is in implementation, not in what counts as done. Decomposability is weak (B6=1): this is one end-to-end path, not fan-out. Net_live lands modestly positive, driven by ordering and horizon rather than by any need for human approval or audit, both of which are pinned out on this corpus.

rows.name: gpt2-codegolf

evidence.B1: "read the .ckpt and the .bpe file" and "sample from the model with arg-max sampling ... continue the output ... for the next 20 tokens" force a chained pipeline inside one file: parse the TF checkpoint index/tensor layout -> map weights into the right matrices -> BPE-encode the input string -> run the ordered transformer stack (LN -> QKV -> causal-masked attention -> residual -> MLP -> residual) -> logits -> argmax -> append token -> re-run. Against that, both live cost dimensions sit at 2: at 45 expert-minutes and a 30-minute agent budget the ceremony is a real fraction of the work (C2), and the packing method cannot be chosen without first inspecting the request-length distributions and the cost model's term structure (C4), so any process encoded up front is partly a guess. rows.name: mailman

evidence.B1: The instruction requires a working postfix+mailman3 pipeline: "You must save mailman configuration file in /etc/mailman3/mailman.cfg" and mail to "reading-group-join@local.edu" must reach the list, with delivery landing in "/var/mail/<username>". The mailman.cfg and the created list/domain are producers whose output (mailman's generated transport/domain maps, the LMTP endpoint) postfix consumes; configuring or reloading postfix before the list exists yields a silently non-delivering server. That is a real producer/consumer dependency inside one deliverable, but the instruction states no explicit first-X-then-Y chain of two or more, so 2 rather than 3.
evidence.B3: metadata expertMinutes = 60, squarely in the ~30-120 minute band; agentTimeoutSec = 1800, far below the 7200 threshold the profile uses for B3=2. Single sitting, one context.
evidence.B5: "An `/app/eval.py` script is provided to help iterations." The agent can run this itself against the three named behaviours (join, leave, post), so it can see how many of them now work and whether a change improved things — a self-computable quantity with feedback, not merely a one-shot pass/fail oracle, and independent of the hidden verifier.
evidence.B6: The three listed functionalities ("reading-group-join", "reading-group-leave", "reading-group" posting) are behaviours of one integrated server configuration sharing mailman.cfg, the same domain/list object and the same postfix transport; they cannot be built or verified independently. Slight separability of the postfix side from the mailman side is the most that exists.
evidence.B8: Several outputs are pinned ("/etc/mailman3/mailman.cfg", "/var/mail/<username>", "SubscriptionPolicy.open"), which narrows the gap, but the deliverable is stated in outcome terms — "Spin up a mailing list server" with "basic mailman3 functionalities" — spanning postfix main.cf, transport/alias maps, mailman core, LMTP and local delivery. Two competent agents would plausibly ship materially different configurations, and one that starts the services and creates the list looks complete while mail silently bounces.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes = 60 falls in the profile's ~30-120 minute band; with agentTimeoutSec = 1800 the whole run is capped at 30 minutes, so per-step mandatory stops are a noticeable fraction of the work without being absurd.
evidence.C4: The instruction does not lead with a symptom and names the stack up front — "using postfix and mailman3 (both are installed already)" — plus the exact policy ("SubscriptionPolicy.open") and delivery target. Wiring mailman3 to postfix via LMTP with local mbox delivery is the conventional documented procedure for this domain; what is open is the tooling/config detail of the preinstalled packages, not the method.

rows.processRecommendation: library/specializations/devops-sre-platform/ composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gate on `python3 /app/eval.py`)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent writes /etc/mailman3/mailman.cfg, creates the domain and list, sees the service start, and declares done — without regenerating mailman's postfix transport/domain maps, running `postmap`, and reloading postfix, so mail to reading-group-join@local.edu bounces or is delivered locally instead of to mailman's LMTP listener.
