rows.rationale: The decisive factor is B1: this is one deliverable with a genuine producer/consumer chain — mailman.cfg and the created domain/list must exist before postfix's transport wiring means anything — and the classic failure is a config that starts cleanly while mail never reaches the list. That is offset by a modest horizon (60 expert-minutes, a 30-minute agent cap) which keeps B3 at 1 and pushes C2 to 2, and by a conventional, well-documented integration method that keeps C4 at 1. B5 earns 2 because /app/eval.py is explicitly offered "to help iterations", giving the agent a self-runnable signal over three distinct behaviours rather than a single oracle. B6 is low: the join/leave/post behaviours are facets of one server configuration, not fan-out. B8 sits at 2 — the paths and policy are pinned, but "spin up a mailing list server" is an outcome-shaped goal spanning postfix and mailman, so a confidently wrong-but-plausible configuration is easy to produce.

rows.name: make-doom-for-mips

evidence.B1: "I've finally provided vm.js that will expect a file called doomgeneric_mips and will run it. Please figure out the rest and build the doomgeneric_mips ELF" — the build configuration (target ISA, endianness, static linking, syscall/libc surface) is only determinable after vm.js and the supplied doomgeneric_img.c are inspected; the toolchain step consumes that derived knowledge, and the run step consumes the resulting ELF. Getting the order wrong (building before establishing what the VM accepts) yields a binary that compiles cleanly but the VM cannot execute.
evidence.B3: task.toml expert_time_estimate = 480 minutes and difficulty = hard, four times the corpus median of 120; the 2-8 hour band. [agent] timeout_sec is only 900, well below the 7200 that would force a 3.
evidence.B5: "so that I can run `node vm.js`. After running `node vm.js` I expect that stdout will be printed appropriately, and frames will be written to the file system" — the agent can execute vm.js itself and observe stdout and /tmp/frame.bmp, giving a self-administered check, but it is pass/fail (does it run, is a frame produced) with no quantity to improve or figure to beat.
evidence.B6: The deliverable is one indivisible artifact — a single "doomgeneric_mips ELF". The sub-activities (toolchain setup, integrating doomgeneric_img.c, satisfying vm.js) are strictly sequential inputs to that one binary, not independently verifiable units that could fan out.
evidence.B8: "Please figure out the rest" and "stdout will be printed appropriately" leave the method and the success bar in outcome terms. The filename and /tmp/frame.bmp path are pinned, but two competent agents could ship materially different binaries (different cross toolchain, libc, syscall shim, static vs. dynamic) and an agent could declare success on a binary that boots and prints banner text without ever confirming that successive frames render — a confident, plausible-looking partial result.
evidence.C2: expert_time_estimate = 480 minutes places this in the 2-8 hour band; orchestration stops are material but do not dominate work of this size. Scored as the mirror of B3=2.
evidence.C4: The instruction supplies inputs that must be read before the method can be chosen: "/app/doomgeneric/, the source code to doom", "a special doomgeneric_img.c that I want you to use", and "vm.js that will expect a file called doomgeneric_mips". It does not lead with a symptom, so not 3, but naming the output file (doomgeneric_mips) says nothing about how to produce it — the toolchain, ABI and syscall approach are discovered by inspecting vm.js and the codebase.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/plan-and-execute.js composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gate on `node vm.js` exiting 0 and /tmp/frame.bmp existing and being a valid BMP)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent installs a MIPS cross-toolchain, gets doomgeneric to compile, sees an ELF named doomgeneric_mips on disk, and reports done — without ever running `node vm.js` end-to-end, so the binary is the wrong endianness/ABI or dynamically linked against a libc the VM has no loader for. The adjacent failure is the agent making `node vm.js` "work" by editing vm.js or stubbing the frame-writing path instead of fixing the build, producing stdout but no valid /tmp/frame.bmp.
rows.rationale: The decisive tension is that the work is long (480 expert-minutes, hard) and its method must be reverse-engineered from supplied inputs — vm.js's expected ISA and syscall surface are never stated — while the deliverable itself is a single indivisible binary with a pinned filename and a pinned output path. That gives moderate ordering value (B1=2: inspect the VM, then configure the build, then produce and run the ELF) and moderate drift risk (B8=2: "figure out the rest" plus "printed appropriately" leaves room to declare victory on a binary that loads but never renders), but no decomposability at all (B6=0) and only a pass/fail self-check rather than a convergence loop (B5=1). On the cost side C4=2 dominates: the procedure genuinely cannot be chosen until vm.js and doomgeneric_img.c are read, so any process encoded up front would be guessing at the build strategy, and C2=1 reflects that orchestration overhead is real but not dominant against multi-hour work. The counterfactual is concrete and not empty — the most likely vanilla failure is skipping the end-to-end `node vm.js` verification, or satisfying it by editing vm.js rather than the binary — which is exactly what a deterministic gate on the VM run would catch. Benefit and cost land close to parity; the orchestrator's net_live will place it near the middle of the corpus.

rows.name: make-mips-interpreter

evidence.B1: "implement a MIPS interpreter complete with handling system calls called vm.js so that I can run `node vm.js` and this should run the MIPS file" — the ELF at /app/doomgeneric_mips must first be parsed and loaded into an emulated memory image before fetch/decode/execute has anything to run on, and register/memory state produced by execution is what the syscall layer and the frame-writing path consume. One step's output is genuinely the next step's input inside the single vm.js deliverable. Scored 2 rather than 3 because the instruction states no explicit phase order and a wrong order fails loudly (nothing runs) rather than silently yielding a plausible-but-wrong result.
evidence.B3: metadata: "expertMinutes": 480, "difficulty": "hard" — squarely at the top of the profile's ~2–8 hour band and 4x the corpus median of 120. Not scored 3: 480 is not "over ~8 hours", the instruction names no distinct artifact-producing phases, and "agentTimeoutSec": 1800 is far below the 7200 trigger, so a resume-across-sittings horizon is not available anyway.
evidence.B5: "along with doomgeneric/, the corresponding source code" and "Running this file should result in saving the frames as they are rendered" — the agent can measure its own progress without the hidden verifier: run vm.js, count how far execution gets before an unimplemented opcode or syscall traps, and compare rendered output against the provided source (which can be built/inspected natively). That is a quantity that visibly improves each iteration. No stated figure to beat, so not 3.
evidence.B6: The deliverable is one file — "implement a MIPS interpreter ... called vm.js". Opcode and syscall handlers are nominally separable but share the decoder, register file and memory model and are only verifiable once the whole loop runs, so there is no genuine parallel fan-out of independently checkable units.
evidence.B8: "this should result in saving the frames as they are rendered, one at a time. I will check that you booted doom correctly, and check that the first frame is correctly created and saved." The outcome is described in outcome terms only: no output path, filename pattern or image format is pinned. Two competent agents would plausibly emit materially different artifacts, and a partially-implemented interpreter can emit a well-formed but blank/garbage first frame that reads as success. Not 3 — the target (boot doom, save first frame) is a single concrete deliverable, not an open-ended goal spanning many systems.
evidence.C2: "expertMinutes": 480 places this in the ~2–8 hour band: orchestration turns and mandatory stops are material but do not dominate a multi-hour emulator implementation. Scored consistently with B3=2.
evidence.C4: "I have provided /app/doomgeneric_mips, a MIPS elf file, along with doomgeneric/, the corresponding source code." The instruction leads with a build request, not a symptom, so not 3 — but the procedure cannot be fixed until those supplied inputs are inspected: which MIPS ISA subset, ABI, relocation/segment layout and which libc syscalls doomgeneric actually issues are all discovered by reading the ELF and the source. Naming vm.js as the output says nothing about the method.

rows.processRecommendation: custom (emulator/interpreter build) composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js and library/methodologies/tdd.js — drive opcode/syscall coverage from a growing set of self-run checks against the provided source before the hidden verifier ever runs
rows.vanillaFailureMode: A vanilla session implements opcodes reactively — adding each instruction only when the interpreter traps on it — burns its context on that loop, and stops once `node vm.js` exits without crashing, writing a first frame that is actually a blank or garbage framebuffer because a file/memory syscall (WAD open/read/lseek) was stubbed rather than implemented. It then reports "doom boots and the first frame is saved" without ever comparing that frame against a rendering derived from the provided doomgeneric/ source, so the silently-wrong artifact ships.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is that this task's difficulty is real but its output contract is loose: the instruction pins the entry point (`node vm.js`) and the success criteria in prose ("booted doom correctly", "first frame is correctly created and saved") without pinning frame path or format, so a partially-implemented interpreter can produce a well-formed but empty artifact that reads as done — that gap is what B8=2 and the counterfactual capture, not the technical depth. Benefit is carried jointly by B1 (load-then-execute-then-syscall-then-emit is a genuine chain inside one file) and B3 (480 expert-minutes, 4x corpus median), with B5=2 because the supplied doomgeneric/ source gives the agent a self-computable progress signal independent of the hidden verifier. Cost is dominated by C4=2: the ISA subset and syscall set are discoverable only by inspecting the supplied ELF and codebase, so any process encoded up front would guess at the method. C2 is only 1 — at eight expert-hours, mandatory stops are affordable. Deliberately not inflated: B6 stays at 1 because vm.js is one indivisible artifact with no parallel fan-out, and B3 stays at 2 because 480 minutes is the top of the band, not past it, and the 1800s agent timeout precludes resumption anyway.

rows.name: mcmc-sampling-stan

evidence.B1: Numbered chain where each step consumes the previous one's output: "Write a Stan file named 'hierarchical_model.stan'" → "Write a R script named '/app/analysis.R', that uses rstan::sampling" → "Extract the posterior samples and compute the posterior means" → "Save your results to these files". The Stan file is an intermediate artifact the R script compiles, and the posterior means are derived from the sampling run. Deviation gives a wrong or absent result, but the dependencies are largely mechanically enforced (you cannot extract samples before sampling), so this is one real chained dependency rather than an order an agent could silently violate.
evidence.B3: metadata: "expertMinutes": 180, "difficulty": "hard" — the ~2–8h band of the profile ladder. Work spans toolchain installation ("Install the RStan package (version 2.32.7) ... and the required dependencies for Stan"), model authoring, and a 4-chain × 100,000-iteration sampling run whose compile-plus-run wall clock is itself substantial. Note the countervailing signal: "agentTimeoutSec": 1800 caps the agent at 30 minutes.
evidence.B5: "You are recommended to use the following settings to get accurate estimations: 4 MCMC chains, 100,000 iterations per chain" — the agent can compute its own convergence quantities from the fit (R-hat, effective sample size, Monte Carlo standard error, agreement of posterior means across the 4 chains) and tell whether an estimate improved, without waiting for the hidden verifier. No stated target figure to beat, so not 3.
evidence.B6: Four required artifacts ('hierarchical_model.stan', '/app/analysis.R', 'posterior_alpha_mean.txt', 'posterior_beta_mean.txt') but they are one coupled pipeline: the R script compiles the Stan file and both .txt values come from the same single sampling run. The only mildly separable unit is the Stan model versus the driver script; no genuine fan-out of independently verifiable units.
evidence.B8: The instruction pins the output contract tightly — exact file paths, "a single number" per file, and the full model specification including "y_i ~ Binomial(n_i, theta_i)", "theta_i ~ Beta(alpha, beta)", and "Prior distribution: (alpha, beta) is proportional to (alpha + beta)^(-5/2)". Format is fully determined, but the content is a number the agent derives, so a mis-specified prior (e.g. omitting the Jacobian under a reparameterization) or an unconverged chain produces a well-formed, plausible-looking, wrong file.
evidence.C2: "expertMinutes": 180 places this in the ~2–8h band: mandatory per-step stops are material but do not dominate a task whose sampling run alone ("4 MCMC chains, 100,000 iterations per chain") consumes serious wall clock. Orchestration overhead is a noticeable but not controlling fraction.
evidence.C4: The instruction states the procedure step by step — the sampler ("uses rstan::sampling"), the settings ("4 MCMC chains", "100,000 iterations per chain", "Set random seed to 1"), and the complete model and prior are all given, so no diagnosis and no inspection of '/app/data.csv' is needed to choose the method. What is open is tooling: pinning "the RStan package (version 2.32.7)" plus "the required dependencies for Stan" (C++ toolchain, StanHeaders/V8 compatibility) and how to encode the improper prior (alpha+beta)^(-5/2) in Stan's target/parameterization.

rows.processRecommendation: custom — an environment-setup → Stan-model → sampling → extraction chain, composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gate on the R script exiting 0 and on convergence diagnostics) and drawing on library/specializations/data-engineering-analytics/
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The concrete failure is a well-formed wrong number. Either (a) the agent burns most of its budget on \"Install the RStan package (version 2.32.7) ... and the required dependencies for Stan\" — a notoriously brittle C++ toolchain install — then, unable to complete the \"4 MCMC chains, 100,000 iterations\" run inside the 1800s agent timeout, writes posterior means from a truncated run, a shortcut approximation, or a plausible guess into '/app/posterior_alpha_mean.txt' and '/app/posterior_beta_mean.txt' and declares success, since the .txt files look identical either way; or (b) it encodes \"(alpha + beta)^(-5/2)\" on a transformed scale without the log-Jacobian correction, producing shifted-but-plausible means with a Stan file that reads correct. Nothing in a vanilla session forces the agent to prove the sampler actually converged before writing the answer files.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is that the answer artifacts are two bare numbers whose correctness is invisible from their format, sitting behind a brittle install step and an expensive sampling run — the classic setup for a premature 'done'. B3=2 (180 expert-minutes, hard, with a toolchain build plus a 4x100k-iteration run) is the top benefit driver, supported by a genuine B1=2 dependency chain (Stan file → rstan::sampling → extracted means → output files) and B5=2, since R-hat/ESS/cross-chain agreement give the agent a quantity it can compute and improve on its own before the verifier ever runs. Cost is low on both live dimensions: the method is dictated step by step in the instruction (sampler, chain count, iterations, seed, full model and prior), so C4=1 covers only the RStan pinning and the Jacobian question, and C2=1 follows the 2–8h anchor. B8 stays at 1 despite the 'hard' label — the instruction pins paths, format and the entire model, so difficulty here is not drift risk; the residual risk is a derived number that looks fine. Net effect is a modestly positive live benefit with C4 as the larger of two small costs.

rows.name: merge-diff-arc-agi-task

evidence.B1: Explicit chained sequence: "mkdir /app/repo, then initialize a git repo" → "Fetch the first git bundle ... into a local branch named branch1" → "Fetch the second git bundle ... branch2" → "At this stage the git repository in /app/repo must contain two branches" → "Use branch1 as the base branch. Merge branch2 into branch1." Each step consumes the artifact the previous step produced (repo → branches → merge result → algo.py present in merged tree). Merging before both branches exist, or merging in the wrong direction, silently yields a wrong repository state that still looks like a merged repo.
evidence.B3: metadata: expertMinutes 20 and agentTimeoutSec 900 (15 minutes). Well under the ~30-minute single-sitting band; no phase here outlives a context window.
evidence.B5: "Verify that algo.py produces the correct outputs for all examples in /app/examples.json." The agent holds the full example set locally and can compute how many example grids its candidate map reproduces element-by-element, iterating on the inferred rule until all match — a self-measurable quantity with feedback, not merely a single pass/fail probe. The hidden test inputs are not evidence (B2 is pinned).
evidence.B6: The two bundle fetches ("the first git bundle located at /app/bundle1.bundle", "the second git bundle located at /app/bundle2.bundle") are mutually independent, but everything after them converges on one merge and one file, "/app/repo/algo.py". No genuine N-way fan-out.
evidence.B8: Output is pinned tightly: path "/app/repo/algo.py", "a function named map that takes a two-dimensional array of integers as input and returns a two-dimensional array", and "outputs matching the expected results exactly, element by element." The only agent-derived content is the inferred mapping rule, which can overfit the visible examples and still look well-formed. Conflict resolution has mild latitude ("a consistent file structure") but the required artifact is named explicitly.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 20 and a 900-second agent timeout put this under the ~30-minute band; a mandatory stop plus gate evaluation after each of the four or five short git commands would cost more turns than the commands themselves.
evidence.C4: The git half states its procedure literally, but the algorithmic half cannot be planned until a supplied input is inspected: "implement the mapping from inputs to outputs as defined by the examples in /app/examples.json" — the rule is latent in a dataset named in the instruction. The instruction also concedes the git path may need inspection ("If fetching from HEAD does not work or is ambiguous, inspect the bundle references"). No symptom-led diagnosis framing, so it stops at the inspect-the-input line rather than 3.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/plan-and-execute.js with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js backing a run-all-examples check
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The likely vanilla failure is the merge step being papered over: hitting conflicts, the agent resolves with `git checkout --ours`/a blanket strategy or simply writes a fresh algo.py into branch1's tree, so branch2's content is silently dropped while the repo still shows a completed merge. The second concrete failure is stopping at partial verification — inferring a mapping rule from the first two or three entries of examples.json, spot-checking one of them, and declaring done without running map over every example, shipping a rule that reproduces the checked grids but not the rest.
rows.rationale: The decisive tension is a genuinely strict dependency chain (B1=3: repo → branch1 → branch2 → merge → algo.py, where wrong order yields a plausible-but-wrong repository) sitting on top of a 20-expert-minute task. Everything else is small: horizon is zero (900s agent timeout), the deliverable is one file with an exactly pinned signature and element-by-element output contract, so drift risk is low despite the ARC-style inference being hard — difficulty is not drift. The counterfactual is concrete and non-empty: conflict resolution that silently discards one branch, and premature "done" after checking a subset of examples.json. Against that, C2=3 (per-step stops dominate a twenty-minute job) and C4=2 (the mapping rule is only discoverable by inspecting the supplied examples) make orchestration overhead the dominant term.

rows.name: model-extraction-relu-logits

evidence.B1: "You do not know the shape of A1" plus "By making queries to forward(), write a file called /app/steal.py" — the recovery pipeline is chained inside one deliverable: probe forward() to locate ReLU kink/critical points, use those points to estimate per-neuron directions, infer the hidden width, then assemble and save the matrix. Later steps consume values produced earlier (critical points feed the finite-difference direction estimates), so a wrong order yields a plausible-but-wrong matrix rather than an error.
evidence.B3: metadata: expertMinutes 480, difficulty "hard" — the 2–8 hour band of the profile ladder; agentTimeoutSec is only 900, so the work is long relative to an expert but bounded per attempt.
evidence.B5: "you can query by importing forward.py and calling forward(x) which returns a single floating point number" and "equal to A1 (up to permuting neurons and scaling)" — the agent can compute its own error signal without the verifier: fit the remaining parameters against its candidate A1 and compare reconstructed outputs to forward(x) on fresh inputs, or measure residuals of estimated hyperplane normals, then reduce that quantity by refining step sizes/query counts. No target figure is stated, so not 3.
evidence.B6: A single deliverable — "write a file called /app/steal.py" saving one array to "/app/stolen_A1.npy". "up to permuting neurons" implies multiple neuron rows that could in principle be recovered independently, but the count is unknown up front and there is no separately verifiable unit, so this is near-indivisible.
evidence.B8: Output is pinned by path and form: "/app/steal.py", "save this matrix to /app/stolen_A1.npy", content "equal to A1 (up to permuting neurons and scaling)". Format is fully determined, but the matrix contents (and its row count) are derived by the agent, so a mis-estimated matrix would still be a well-formed .npy that looks complete.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 480 sits in the 2–8 hour band; per-step mandatory stops are material but do not dominate work of this size, and agentTimeoutSec 900 leaves little slack for ceremony.
evidence.C4: The instruction names the artifacts exactly but not the method: "You do not know the shape of A1, but it returns a single float" — the hidden width and the usable query regime can only be established by probing the supplied forward.py black box, and the attack procedure (where to search for critical points, what step sizes survive float noise) is chosen after that inspection. No symptom-led diagnosis, so not 3.

rows.processRecommendation: custom (a query-probe → critical-point search → direction-estimation → reconstruction-error convergence loop, composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js on a self-written reconstruction check)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: A vanilla agent fits a plausible matrix by naive finite-difference gradients at random points (or least squares against a guessed width), writes a well-formed /app/stolen_A1.npy with the wrong number of rows or rows that are not the true hyperplane normals, and declares success without ever running the self-check that is available to it — refitting the outer parameters and comparing reconstructed forward outputs to the real forward(x) on fresh inputs. The skipped step is that reconstruction check; the artifact is silently wrong but looks correct.
rows.rationale: The decisive live factors are the chained internal pipeline (B1=2) and the 480-minute expert estimate (B3=2): recovering A1 requires probing forward() for critical points, deriving neuron directions from those points, and only then assembling the matrix, and a wrong order produces a plausible matrix rather than a crash. B5=2 because the agent has a genuine self-measurable error — reconstruct forward(x) from its candidate parameters and compare — which a convergence loop could exploit, and this is exactly the check a vanilla run is most likely to skip. Against that, C4=2 dominates the cost side: the instruction fixes the artifacts but not the method, and the hidden width plus the numerical regime must be discovered by querying the black box before any procedure can be encoded, so a prematurely fixed process risks encoding the wrong attack. B6=1 (one indivisible script) and B8=1 (path, format, and equivalence criterion all pinned; difficulty is not drift) keep the benefit side from rising further. C2=1 reflects that orchestration overhead is noticeable but not dominant at this task size.

evidence.B1: Chained dependencies: step 2 produces `/app/ssl/server.key`, step 3's self-signed cert is generated from that key, step 4's `server.pem` is 'a combined PEM file that includes both the private key and certificate', and step 5's `verification.txt` contains the subject/validity/SHA-256 fingerprint derived from the cert produced in step 3. evidence.B3: `expertMinutes: 20` and `agentTimeoutSec: 900` (15 minutes) — far under the ~30-minute line; a handful of openssl invocations plus one short Python script in a single sitting.
evidence.B5: The agent can self-check pass/fail — it can re-read the artifacts (`openssl x509 -noout -subject -dates -fingerprint -sha256`) and run its own `/app/check_cert.py`, which is required to print 'Certificate verification successful' if all checks pass. That is a binary check with no scale or quantity to improve toward.
evidence.B6: Once the key and cert exist, `/app/ssl/verification.txt` (step 5) and `/app/check_cert.py` (step 6) are independent of each other, but everything else is one serial chain of five files in a single directory — a couple of separable leaves, not genuine fan-out.
evidence.B8: Paths (`/app/ssl/server.key`, `server.crt`, `server.pem`, `verification.txt`, `/app/check_cert.py`), key size (2048-bit RSA), permissions (600), validity (365 days), Organization Name ('DevOps Team'), Common Name ('dev-internal.company.local'), and the exact success string are all pinned. Residual latitude is only in content the agent derives and formats — 'validity dates in YYYY-MM-DD format or OpenSSL format with optional timezone' explicitly admits variants, and the verification.txt layout is unspecified, so a mis-formatted date or fingerprint would still look well-formed.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 20`, `difficulty: medium`, `agentTimeoutSec: 900` — under the ~30-minute line; a mandatory stop plus gate turn after each of six short steps costs more than issuing the openssl commands themselves.

Whether the true password is among the lines is knowable only from the hidden verifier, and 'You are allowed to make multiple guesses' removes any need to converge on one best answer.

evidence.B8: Output is pinned to an exact path and line format ('one per line, to the file: /app/recovered_passwords.txt') and content is constrained by four explicit properties (length 23, 8XD prefix, W54 suffix, uppercase+digits), so a wrong answer is narrow in shape. Residual risk is only that derived content is wrong — a fabricated or brute-forced 23-char string satisfies every stated constraint and looks correct.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes: 100 sits in the ~30-120 band; with agentTimeoutSec: 900 the run is short, so a mandatory stop after each of a handful of steps is a noticeable fraction of the total work.
evidence.C4: The deliverable is named exactly but no method is stated — only the goal 'recover the PASSWORD from the deleted file'. Which technique applies (raw block-device grep, inode/journal scan, /proc/*/fd on a process still holding the handle, free-space scan) cannot be chosen until the supplied environment — the /app filesystem and how it is backed inside the container — has been inspected.

The benefit that does exist is ordering — carve must precede filter, and filtering an incomplete dump produces a plausible empty or short file (B1=2). Everything else is small: one indivisible output file (B6=0), an exactly pinned path and format with four explicit content constraints holding drift down (B8=1), and only a pass/fail self-check per candidate with no measurable progress signal (B5=1). The counterfactual is concrete and non-empty — the agent greps, finds nothing, and fabricates format-conforming strings — but that single failure does not carry enough weight against C2+C4 to make orchestration pay here.

One dependency chain inside a single deliverable, not two or more.

The agent can compile, run, and compute the same L2 metric against /app/image.ppm itself (the read prohibition applies to image.c, not to the agent), and can run the gzip check directly — a measurable quantity with an explicit target of 0.99 and headroom, i.e. a defined finish line.

Format and contract are fully determined, but the pixel content is derived by the agent — a renderer that reproduces the wrong scene still compiles and emits a well-formed PPM, so a failure looks finished.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 360 sits in the ~2-8 hour band; per-step mandatory stops are material but do not dominate six hours of render-and-compare work. Scored consistently with B3=2.

Which rendering approach, geometry and material model to encode cannot be chosen until that image is inspected. The instruction does not lead with a symptom or complaint, so line 3 does not fire.

No empty lines", a fixed N-to-C order, no start/stop codons, no terminal linkers, explicit length and GC bounds. The gap left open is content the agent derives — codon choice, linker composition, and which fluorophore/binder it picks — so a wrong choice still produces a well-formed sequence that reads as complete. No ordering dependency and nothing to fan out (B1=1, B6=0), and the only self-check available is pass/fail on cases the agent constructs itself (B5=1). The counterfactual is concrete - an untested regex that breaks on the trailing-date or boundary traps - but mandatory stops do not fix that; only running the pattern against edge cases does, which fits in one vanilla context. Shape is conventional (C4=1), so an encoded process would reduce to write-regex-then-test-regex plus journaling overhead.

rows.name: reshard-c4-data

evidence.B1: decompress.py must invert whatever encoding compress.py produces: 'Should reconstruct the original file structure and content exactly'. The second deliverable consumes a format defined by the first, so designing them out of order yields a decompressor that cannot reverse the shard format. Also the uv venv + pyproject.toml must exist before dependencies are usable ('all required dependencies can be installed by running `uv sync` in /app'). One real chained dependency, not two or more.
evidence.B3: metadata: expertMinutes 30, difficulty 'medium', agentTimeoutSec 3600 (one hour, well under the 7200 threshold for a 2). Two small scripts plus a round-trip test on a provided sample slice — a single sitting.
evidence.B5: The agent can measure its own success locally and iterate: the constraints are stated numbers it can compute over its own output ('Maximum 30 files or folders in each directory', 'Maximum 15MB filesize per file'), and the round-trip target is exact ('reconstruct the original file structure and content exactly') against the provided c4_sample/ data. Compress, count entries, stat sizes, decompress, diff against the original — a defined finish line reachable by self-scored iteration without the hidden verifier.
evidence.B6: Two named deliverables (/app/compress.py and /app/decompress.py) plus the uv/pyproject setup, but they are tightly coupled inverses — decompress cannot be written or validated independently of compress's format. Not genuine fan-out; effectively one artifact with two entry points.
evidence.B8: Output is pinned hard: exact paths ('/app/compress.py', '/app/decompress.py'), exact CLI contracts ('python /app/compress.py <input_dir> <output_dir>', 'python /app/decompress.py <resharded_dir>'), numeric constraints (30 entries, 15MB), exact-reconstruction requirement, and a mandated packaging mechanism (uv venv + pyproject.toml). The intermediate shard format is the agent's choice, so an error would still look well-formed, but the contract leaves little room for two materially different satisfying artifacts.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 30 with agentTimeoutSec 3600: writing two short scripts and a pyproject.toml. At the low end of the 30-120 minute band, so mandatory per-step stops and journaling are a noticeable fraction of the total work. Scored consistently with B3=1.
evidence.C4: The procedure cannot be fixed until the supplied input is inspected: 'You should develop and test your scripts using the provided slice of my data in the c4_sample/ directory' and 'my other slices, which are structured, sized, and distributed similarly'. The packing strategy (how to group, whether to concatenate, split, or compress) depends on the actual file sizes, counts and nesting depth of c4_sample, which the instruction never states. Not a symptom-led diagnosis task, so it does not reach 3.

rows.processRecommendation: library/specializations/data-engineering-analytics/ composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gates: round-trip hash equality, a constraint scan for >30 entries / >15MB, and a clean `uv sync && uv run` check)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: A vanilla agent writes compress.py, eyeballs that the output directory looks plausible, and declares done without ever executing the full round trip — so the silently wrong artifact is a decompress.py that restores directory structure but not byte-identical content (the fixture files_hashes.json implies exact hash equality), or a compressor that satisfies the 15MB cap but leaves some directory over 30 entries at a nesting level it never checked. The second likely skip is the packaging clause: it pip-installs a dependency into the ambient environment and never verifies that a clean `uv sync` in /app followed by `uv run` installs nothing further.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is that this is a small, exactly-specified two-script deliverable — 30 expert-minutes, a one-hour agent budget, pinned paths, pinned CLI signatures and pinned numeric constraints — so the ceremony cost (C2=2) plus the need to inspect c4_sample before the packing strategy can be chosen (C4=2) together outweigh a modest benefit side. The one strong benefit is B5=3: the agent can fully self-score its work locally by counting directory entries, stat-ing file sizes, and diffing a decompressed tree against the original, which is exactly the loop a convergence process would enforce. B1=2 because decompress.py is the inverse of a format compress.py defines, so design order is real, but that is a single dependency inside one small unit of work rather than a multi-phase pipeline. B8 is low, not high: the long list of explicit constraints narrows the gap between plausible answers rather than widening it, and difficulty is not drift risk. A concrete vanilla failure exists — skipping the round-trip verification or the clean `uv sync` check — so the counterfactual is not empty, but it is the kind of check a competent single session often performs unprompted.

rows.name: rstan-to-pystan

evidence.B1: The instruction imposes a data-flow chain: "Read the provided R script '/app/gp_rstan.R' to figure out the stan model structure, and hyperparameters used for posterior sampling" -> "Convert the R script to a Python script" -> "Run your converted script to do posterior sampling. Extract the posterior samples and compute the posterior means. Save the results". The extracted model/hyperparameters are a derived value consumed by the later script, and the posterior draws are consumed by the CSV write; writing the Python model before faithfully reading the R source silently yields a plausible-but-different posterior. One dependency chain, not two independent ones, so 2 rather than 3.
evidence.B3: metadata `expertMinutes: 180` (3 hours) falls in the profile's ~2-8 hour band; `difficulty: medium`. Counter-signal: `agentTimeoutSec: 1800` is only 30 minutes, well under the 7200 that would independently justify 2, so the horizon is scored on expert time alone.
evidence.B5: "your converted Stan model code is functionally equivalent to the original stan model in R script" and "Given the same data, your converted script should do exactly the same posterior sampling as the original R script" give a reference to compare against - but the agent is explicitly barred from executing it ("You are NOT allowed to run the provided R script"), so the comparison is a static pass/fail reading of the Stan block, not a quantity it can compute and watch improve. The optional "optimize the Stan model for memory efficiency" is unmeasured against any target.
evidence.B6: One deliverable, '/app/pystan_analysis.py', and a single sampling run; the four outputs (alpha_est.csv, sigma_est.csv, rho_est.csv, beta_est.csv) are all posterior means extracted from that same fit, so there is nothing to fan out or verify independently.
evidence.B8: The output contract is pinned exactly - four named paths, "single number", "3 numbers, one per row", "Save only the numeric values for CSV files" - plus hard constraints ("must use PyStan 3.10.0", "NOT allowed to use cmdstanr or cmdstanpy", "you must set the random_seed to 1"). The format is fixed but the numeric content is derived by the agent, so a mis-transcribed prior or sampler setting produces a well-formed file with wrong numbers.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 180` sits in the profile's ~2-8 hour band: orchestration turns are material but do not dominate a task whose sampling run alone consumes real wall-clock (`verifierTimeoutSec: 1800`).
evidence.C4: The instruction does not state the model; it says "Read the provided R script '/app/gp_rstan.R' to figure out the stan model structure, and hyperparameters used for posterior sampling". The Stan blocks, priors, kernel form and sampler settings cannot be chosen until that supplied file - and /app/meta_public.json - are inspected. Naming the four output CSVs does not settle the method (profile: naming outputs says nothing about C4). Not 3: the instruction leads with a procedure, not a symptom.

rows.processRecommendation: library/specializations/code-migration-modernization/ composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent skims gp_rstan.R, reproduces the GP kernel and priors approximately, and quietly drops or defaults one of the sampling settings (chains/iter/warmup/adapt_delta, or the required `random_seed=1` on `stan.build`), then writes four well-formed CSVs of posterior means from a differently-parameterized model and declares success - the artifacts look exactly right and the divergence is invisible without a line-by-line diff against the R source, which the agent is forbidden to run.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is that the model specification is hidden inside a supplied file the agent may read but not execute, so both the ordering benefit (B1=2: extract-then-convert-then-sample-then-write, with a real silent-corruption mode) and the shape uncertainty cost (C4=2) come from the same fact - the procedure is only knowable after inspecting /app/gp_rstan.R. Horizon is moderate (B3=2 on 180 expert-minutes, though the 1800s agent timeout argues the agent's own run is short) and overhead is correspondingly middling (C2=1). Drift risk is low (B8=1): the instruction pins four output paths, their formats, the library version, and the seed, so a confident wrong answer can only differ in the numbers, not in the artifact. Decomposability is nil (B6=0) - one script, one fit - and convergence value is weak (B5=1) because the only reference is a script the agent is explicitly forbidden to run, leaving no self-computable quantity to iterate on.

rows.name: sam-cell-seg

evidence.B1: The single script has a real internal data dependency chain: masks must be produced from the bbox prompts ('xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax ... the mask'), then the global constraint 'there should be no overlap between masks and each cell must have only one contiguous mask' must be resolved across all masks, and only then can 'coords_x'/'coords_y' and the 'updated xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax' columns be derived from the final mask. Extracting coordinates or recomputing the bounding box before de-overlapping yields a plausible-but-wrong CSV. The instruction states no explicit step order, so this is a derived-value dependency rather than an explicit first-X-then-Y-then-Z.
evidence.B3: metadata: expertMinutes 600 (10 hours) and agentTimeoutSec 7200 — over the ~8-hour line in the profile's B3 ladder; the corpus median is 120.
evidence.B5: The agent can compute its own quality signals on the supplied demo files ('/app/demo_rgb.png', '/app/demo_metadata.csv') and iterate: count overlapping pixels between masks and count connected components per mask, against the stated finish lines 'there should be no overlap between masks' and 'each cell must have only one contiguous mask', plus 'The resulting masks should all be polylines (not rectangular)'. These are measurable quantities with an explicit target of zero violations, not something knowable only from the hidden verifier.
evidence.B6: One deliverable: 'You must write a python script in /app named convert_masks.py'. There is mild separability (MobileSAM weight loading/inference vs. post-processing vs. CSV round-trip) but no set of independently verifiable units to fan out; the per-cell masks are runtime iteration inside one artifact, not parallel work units.
evidence.B8: The output contract is tightly pinned — exact script path, exact argparse flags ('--weights_path', '--output_path', '--rgb_path', '--csv_path'), and 'a csv that matches the input csv (just with updated xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, coords_x, and coords_y columns)' — plus hard constraints ('must use MobileSAM', 'can not use the original SAM model', 'Do not modify MobileSAM source code', 'must run on CPU', fixed package list). Format is fully determined; only the mask contents are agent-derived, so a wrong result would still be well-formed.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 600 — above the ~8-hour anchor, so mandatory per-step stops are a rounding error against the work; agentTimeoutSec is 7200.
evidence.C4: The procedure cannot be fixed until supplied inputs are inspected: the agent must examine '/app/demo_metadata.csv' to learn how 'coords_x'/'coords_y' encode 'the polyline or bounding box' and which rows are rectangles, and inspect the named external codebase 'https://github.com/ChaoningZhang/MobileSAM' to learn its prompting API. It does not lead with a symptom requiring diagnosis — the goal ('convert all of the masks to polylines') and the deliverable are stated — but the post-processing method for de-overlapping and enforcing contiguity is discovered by looking at the data.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/plan-and-execute.js composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gate on a self-written checker over the demo files: zero inter-mask overlap, one connected component per cell, no rectangular coords, bbox columns consistent with coords)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent gets MobileSAM loading on CPU and producing a per-cell mask from each row's bounding box, eyeballs the result on demo_rgb.png, and declares success — silently skipping the two global post-conditions that are not visible in a single-cell spot check: cross-mask overlap removal and enforcement of one contiguous component per cell (SAM box prompts routinely return multi-blob masks and neighbouring cells' masks intersect). A second, quieter variant: it writes the new coords_x/coords_y but carries the original xmin/xmax/ymin/ymax through unchanged, producing a CSV that reads as complete and matches the input schema while the bbox columns no longer describe the refined polyline.
rows.rationale: Horizon dominates: 600 expert-minutes and a 7200-second agent timeout put this at the top of the corpus B3 ladder, and the same anchor drives C2 to 0, so orchestration overhead is negligible against the work. The task also offers a genuine convergence loop — the agent can measure inter-mask overlap and per-cell connected components on the provided demo files against explicit zero-violation targets, so it can improve before the verifier ever runs. Working against that, C4=2 because the encoding of coords_x/coords_y and the MobileSAM prompting API must both be inspected before the post-processing method can be chosen, and B8 is only 1 — the argparse signature, script path, and output schema are pinned exactly, so difficulty here is not drift. B1=2 for the derived-value chain (de-overlap before contour extraction before bbox recomputation) inside the single script, and B6=1 since there is one indivisible deliverable. The counterfactual is concrete: the global no-overlap and contiguity post-conditions are exactly what a vanilla session declares done without, since a single-cell visual check cannot see them.

rows.name: sanitize-git-repo

evidence.B1: "Please find and remove all such information and replace it with placeholder values" — a natural inspect-then-edit reading order (locate the secrets, then substitute placeholders), but no step's output is consumed as an intermediate artifact by a later step, and editing files in a different order changes nothing. Nothing downstream silently breaks on reordering.
evidence.B3: metadata `expertMinutes: 30` and `agentTimeoutSec: 900` (15 minutes) — at the bottom of the corpus range (median 120 expert-minutes) and far below the 7200s timeout that would indicate a multi-sitting horizon. A focused single sitting; nothing in the instruction has distinct phases producing artifacts for a later phase.
evidence.B5: "Please ensure that the sensitive values are not present in the repository after the sanitization" — the agent can re-grep the repo for the captured values and get a pass/fail answer itself. But it is a binary presence check with no scale or target to iterate toward; there is no quantity to improve.
evidence.B6: The test file listing (`process.py`, `ray_cluster.yaml`, `rw_v2_..._arcade100k.json`) implies a handful of contaminated files that could in principle be edited independently, and the instruction lists several distinct credential types (AWS key id, AWS secret, GitHub token, Huggingface token). But it is one repo-wide sweep whose scoping step must be done once and centrally, not genuine N-way fan-out.
evidence.B8: Placeholder format is pinned exactly (`<your-aws-access-key-id>`) and the instruction adds a narrowing constraint — "be careful to not delete or modify any files that are not contaminated". But the credential set is enumerated open-endedly ("For example:", "all API keys"), and "not present in the repository" leaves it undetermined whether git history/packed objects are in scope. Two competent agents plausibly ship materially different artifacts — one rewriting history, one only the working tree, with different judgments about which strings count as secrets — and both would read as complete.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 30` with `agentTimeoutSec: 900`; the actual work is a grep sweep and a few in-place substitutions. Per-step mandatory stops and journal writes would cost more turns than the edits themselves.
evidence.C4: The instruction does not lead with a symptom — it states the goal and the replacement convention — but the procedure cannot be fixed until the supplied repository ("my github repository \"dclm\"") is inspected: which files are contaminated, which credential formats appear, and whether the secrets sit in history as well as the working tree are all discovered by looking. Only the substitution convention is stated, not the method for finding the targets.

rows.processRecommendation: library/specializations/security-compliance/
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent greps for the obvious `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=`/`hf_`/`ghp_` patterns, edits the visible occurrences in `process.py` and `ray_cluster.yaml`, and declares done — leaving the same literal value embedded in the large JSON config or still reachable in git history/packed objects, so the verifier's "value absent from the repository" check fails on a repo that looks clean to a reviewer.
rows.rationale: A 30-expert-minute, 15-minute-timeout sweep whose entire work product is a handful of string substitutions: C2=3 dominates, and orchestration ceremony would exceed the edits themselves. The only real benefit signal is B8=2 — the credential list is explicitly open-ended ("For example") and "not present in the repository" leaves working-tree-vs-history scope undetermined, so a confident partial sanitization reads as complete. That is a genuine and nameable failure, so the counterfactual is not empty, but it is a single-checkpoint risk that one completeness re-grep addresses, not something needing an enforced multi-step process. B1=1 and B3=0: no step consumes another's output, and the task fits one sitting. C4=2 because the contaminated files and secret formats must be discovered by inspecting the supplied repo before the sweep can be planned.

rows.name: schemelike-metacircular-eval

evidence.B1: "a metacircular evaluator capable of interpreting the scheme-like language implemented by interp.py" — the agent must read interp.py (and test/) to learn the exact dialect before writing eval.scm, but that is the ordinary inspect-then-write reading order; there is no chain of intermediate artifacts, and deviating does not silently corrupt a downstream step. The self-hosting constraint ("interpret ... (2) itself") couples the artifact to itself rather than imposing a step sequence.
evidence.B3: metadata expertMinutes = 300 (5 hours), which lands in the profile's ~2–8 hour band; agentTimeoutSec is 2400, below the 7200 threshold, so 2 rather than 3.
evidence.B5: The instruction supplies an executable reference baseline and an exact finish line: "the following three commands should all do the same thing" plus "should be able to interpret (1) each of the test programs in test/, and (2) itself." The agent can itself run `python3 interp.py test/X.scm` versus `python3 interp.py eval.scm` for every file in test/ (test.sh is present), count how many match, and iterate until all match and the third self-interpreting command also matches — a countable quantity with a stated target.
evidence.B6: The deliverable is a single file, "Write a file eval.scm". Individual special forms and primitives are loosely separable units each exercised by a distinct test/ program, but self-interpretation couples them into one indivisible artifact; this is not genuine fan-out.
evidence.B8: Output path, invocation contract and I/O behaviour are pinned: "read exactly one line from STDIN, this will be a file path", "Remaining input should be redirected to the interpreted-program, and any output from the program should be sent back to STDOUT", with three worked command equivalences. The internal design of the evaluator is the agent's, so a partial evaluator can still look well-formed and complete — format pinned, content derived.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes = 300 (5 hours) falls in the ~2–8 hour band: per-step orchestration stops are material but do not dominate work of this size.
evidence.C4: The instruction does not lead with a symptom and does not state the procedure. The target language is defined only by a supplied input that must be inspected first — "the scheme-like language implemented by interp.py" — so which special forms, primitives, tail-call and read/IO semantics must be implemented is unknowable until interp.py and the test/ corpus have been read. That is the profile's line-2 case.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/tdd.js paired with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gate on a loop comparing `python3 interp.py test/X.scm` against the one- and two-level eval.scm invocations for every file in test/)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent gets all of test/ passing under `python3 interp.py eval.scm` and declares done, never closing the self-hosting loop — the third command, `echo -e 'eval.scm\ntest/calculator.scm\n(+ 7 8)' | python3 interp.py eval.scm`. Self-interpretation requires eval.scm to be written entirely within the subset it implements (and to survive the compounding slowdown), so an evaluator that uses a form it never implemented, or that handles the STDIN file-path read in a way that breaks one level down, looks complete and passes the visible tests while failing the shadow_test suite.
rows.rationale: The decisive live factor is B5: the instruction hands the agent its own oracle — interp.py run directly on each test/ program is the reference, and the three worked commands define an exact finish line including self-interpretation, so quality is reachable by a scored iterate-until-all-match loop the agent can run unaided. B3=2 (300 expert-minutes) adds real horizon, but the artifact is a single file with a tightly pinned I/O contract, so B6 and B8 stay at 1 — difficulty here is high while the space of plausible-but-different valid answers is narrow. On cost, C4=2 dominates: the dialect exists only inside interp.py and must be reverse-engineered before any process could be encoded, and C2=1 reflects five hours of work against which mandatory stops are noticeable but not overwhelming. The counterfactual is concrete: the self-hosting level is the step most likely skipped, since the visible test/ suite can be fully green while the two-level invocation is broken.

rows.name: sparql-university

evidence.B1: The three criteria are not independent clauses writable in any order: criterion 3 ("at least one has more than 10 students currently enrolled in any classes taught in that department") requires a per-department aggregate computed and thresholded (subquery + COUNT/HAVING) before it can be joined against the professor/department pattern, since the outer projection groups by ?professorName. Misplacing the aggregation stage silently counts over the wrong grouping key. The reference-date semantics ("Use 2025-08-16 as the reference (today) date wherever needed") must likewise be resolved into the enrollment patterns before the aggregate is taken. Two dependent stages, not a longer chain, so 2.
evidence.B3: metadata `expertMinutes: 800` (over 8 hours) with `difficulty: hard`. Countervailing signal noted: `agentTimeoutSec: 900` (15 minutes) bounds the agent run well inside one sitting, so the expert estimate is the only long-horizon evidence.
evidence.B5: The full graph is local — "a Turtle file at `/app/university_graph.ttl` containing both the ontology and the instance data" — so the agent can run its own query and hand-check individual professors against the triples. That is a whether-it-is-right check with no scale: no stated figure to beat and no reference output to converge toward.
evidence.B6: One deliverable: "Save your query in `/app/solution.sparql`" with a fixed projection. The three enumerated criteria can be prototyped as separate fragments but must be fused into a single query — mild internal structure, not genuine fan-out.
evidence.B8: The output contract is pinned tightly: exact path `/app/solution.sparql`, the exact projection `SELECT ?professorName (GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT ?country; separator=", ") AS ?countries)`, an explicit reference date, and an explicit encoding note ("countries are represented using their two-letter ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes ... Greece is represented as \"GR\""). Content is still agent-derived (EU member list, date predicates, distinct-student counting semantics), so a wrong query still parses and returns a well-formed table. Format pinned, content derived.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 800`, above the ~8-hour anchor, so mandatory per-step stops are a rounding error against the work; scored as the mirror of B3=3. Caveat: `agentTimeoutSec: 900` means the realized agent budget is 15 minutes, under which orchestration turns would dominate — recorded in missing_information.
evidence.C4: The instruction names the input but not the vocabulary: "a Turtle file at `/app/university_graph.ttl` containing both the ontology and the instance data". Predicates for full-professor rank, works-in, teaches, and enrollment dates are unknown until the supplied graph is inspected, so the query shape cannot be chosen up front. It does not lead with a symptom or complaint, so not 3.

rows.processRecommendation: library/specializations/data-engineering-analytics/ with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js backing an execute-the-query-against-the-local-graph check
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent skims the head of the TTL, guesses predicate names and the encoding of "full professor" instead of enumerating the actual ontology, then writes a query it never executes against `/app/university_graph.ttl`. Two things go silently wrong in a well-formed result table: the >10-students check counts enrollment rows or students per class rather than DISTINCT students per department, and the 2025-08-16 currency filter is dropped from enrollment/employment intervals so expired records are counted. The file saves, the SPARQL parses, and the agent declares done.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is B3: `expertMinutes: 800` is the only long-horizon signal in the metadata and sits above the profile's 8-hour anchor, which simultaneously drives C2 to 0 and leaves C4=2 carrying the whole cost side. Everything else is modest — one output file with an exactly pinned projection and path holds B8 to 1 and B6 to 1, and the local graph affords only a pass/fail self-check (B5=1). B1=2 is real rather than cosmetic: the per-department student aggregate is a derived value the outer professor grouping consumes, so the wrong order gives a plausible wrong answer rather than an error. The counterfactual is concrete — guessed predicates plus dropped date-currency filtering produce a well-formed but wrong result set — so no cap applies. The 800-minute versus 900-second contradiction is the single fact most likely to change this scoring.

rows.name: sqlite-db-truncate

evidence.B5: "Recover as many of the rows as possible" — the agent can count the rows it has decoded from the truncated file and tell whether a second parsing pass recovered more, so there is a self-measurable quantity with a direction of improvement. evidence.B6: One input file (/app/trunc.db) and one output file (/app/recover.json). The instruction names no independent units, cases or targets that could be worked in parallel and verified alone — it is a single indivisible recovery artifact.

evidence.C4: The cause is already supplied ("corrupted through binary truncation"), so this is not symptom-first diagnosis, but the recovery procedure cannot be chosen until the supplied input is inspected: how much of /app/trunc.db survived determines whether sqlite3 .recover, page-level b-tree cell walking, or raw record-header scavenging is the right method.

The one genuine benefit signal is the pair B5=2 / B8=2 — "recover as many of the rows as possible" is both a self-measurable quantity the agent can iterate against and the exact clause that lets a partial answer pass as complete, which is the concrete vanilla failure named above. But there is no ordering chain (B1=1), no fan-out (B6=0), and no horizon problem (B3=1), so the enforcement machinery would be paying for one thing only: a completeness gate that stops the agent from banking the first page and leaving. That is a real but narrow payoff against material overhead.

evidence.B1: "Compile SQLite in /app/sqlite with gcov instrumentation" from "/app/vendor/sqlite-fossil-release.tar.gz" implies a chain where each step consumes the prior one's output: extract the vendored tarball → configure with coverage flags → build → expose on PATH. Two competent agents could ship materially different builds that both read as satisfying the sentence.

rows.processRecommendation: library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent passes coverage flags to the compiler but not the linker (or builds the amalgamation with plain CFLAGS), gets a working `sqlite3` on PATH, verifies `sqlite3 --version` succeeds, and declares done — the binary emits no .gcda data at runtime, so the coverage requirement is silently unmet. A second variant: it installs a distro/system sqlite3 onto PATH ahead of the instrumented build in /app/sqlite, so the PATH check passes against the wrong binary.
rows.rationale: A short, conventional build task: untar a pre-vendored SQLite snapshot, compile it with gcov instrumentation, and put it on PATH, at 30 expert-minutes inside a 900-second agent budget. The dominant cost is C2=3 — orchestration stops would outweigh the handful of build commands — with C4 low because the method is standard for a C project and the source is supplied rather than discovered. The real benefit signal is B1=2: coverage flags must be in place before compilation, and getting that order wrong produces a functioning-but-uninstrumented binary rather than a visible error, which is exactly the vanilla failure mode named above. B8=2 because \"with gcov instrumentation\" is stated in outcome terms and leaves the instrumentation scope and artifact locations to the agent. Horizon and decomposability contribute nothing: one artifact, one sitting.

rows.name: torch-pipeline-parallelism

evidence.B1: The instruction prescribes an explicit chained order inside one function: "Partition the model layers in a roughly balanced way. Run forward computation on all microbatches. Run backward computation on all microbatches" and restates it as "Run forward passes for all microbatches first, then run backward passes." The partition determines which layers each rank owns (consumed by forward), forward produces the cached per-microbatch activations and the P2P-received hidden states that backward consumes, and AFAB scheduling itself is an ordering contract — an interleaved (1F1B) or per-microbatch forward+backward loop still trains and still looks correct, but the activations the test's hooks compare against the reference are produced in the wrong order/with wrong buffering. Two or more dependencies chained, violation silently plausible-but-wrong.
evidence.B3: metadata expertMinutes: 240 (4 hours), difficulty "hard" — inside the profile's ~2–8 hour band for B3=2. agentTimeoutSec is 900, below the 7200 trigger, so no bump to 3.
evidence.B5: "The correctness of your implementation will be tested by comparing forward and backward activations against a reference model." The reference is not hidden machinery — it is the unmodified LlamaForCausalLM the agent already has, so the agent can build the non-pipelined baseline itself and compute a numeric activation/gradient delta per microbatch and drive it toward zero, and can additionally check the "world_size values of 1, 2" cases against each other. That is a self-computable quantity that can be seen to improve, with no stated target figure, so 2 rather than 3.
evidence.B6: The deliverable is one file with one entry point: "Create the file /app/pipeline_parallel.py and implement the following function ... def train_step_pipeline_afab(...)". The sub-pieces (layer partitioning, P2P send/recv wiring, last-rank cross_entropy scaling) are loosely separable but share the same tensor-shape and dtype contract and cannot be verified apart from the whole step. Single indivisible artifact with several requirements.
evidence.B8: The output contract is pinned hard: exact path (/app/pipeline_parallel.py), exact signature, exact shapes ("[microbatch, seq_len]", "[microbatch, seq_len, hidden_size]", "Backward tensors use the same shape as the hidden states"), exact loss rule ("compute cross_entropy loss against the targets and scale it by the number of microbatches"), an explicit prohibition ("You must not use hooks inside your implementation"), and the API to use (get_rank/get_world_size, P2POp). Format and interface are fully determined; only the internal implementation is derived by the agent, so an error would still be well-formed. The long constraint list narrows rather than widens the gap.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 240 sits in the profile's ~2–8 hour band: orchestration turns are material but do not dominate four hours of distributed-training implementation and numerical debugging. Scored as the mirror of B3=2.
evidence.C4: The instruction states the method rather than a symptom: partition, all-forward, all-backward, use get_rank/get_world_size, hidden states between stages, cross_entropy scaled by microbatch count on the last rank. No supplied dataset, log or unknown codebase must be inspected before choosing an approach. Only a tooling choice is left open — "Communication between pipeline stages may be implemented with torch.distributed.P2POp" is permissive, not prescriptive — which is the C4=1 line.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/tdd.js composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js — with an added gate step that runs the implementation under both world_size=1 and world_size=2 against a locally-built single-process reference; no existing specialization covers distributed-training schedule implementation, so this is a candidate for a new library/specializations/ml-systems/ entry.
rows.vanillaFailureMode: A vanilla agent writes a loop that does forward-then-backward per microbatch (or 1F1B interleaving), which trains fine and reports no error, but violates the stated AFAB schedule so the hook-captured activation ordering diverges from the reference; a second common variant is receiving the inter-stage hidden state without setting requires_grad/retaining the graph, so gradients silently stop at the stage boundary and only rank 0's layers update. Both are invisible under world_size=1, which degenerates to ordinary single-process training — so the agent verifies the easy case, sees it pass, and declares done without ever exercising world_size=2.
rows.rationale: The decisive live dimension is B1: AFAB is itself an ordering contract, and the instruction chains partition -> all-forward -> all-backward with each step consuming the previous one's output, so a reordering yields a trained-looking but reference-divergent result. B3=2 and B5=2 add real weight — four expert-hours, and a self-constructible reference comparison the agent can iterate against numerically. Costs are low on both live dimensions: the method is spelled out step by step (C4=1, only the P2P primitive is left to choice), and orchestration overhead is a modest fraction of a four-hour task (C2=1). B8 is deliberately held at 1 despite the task's difficulty: path, signature, shapes, loss scaling and the no-hooks prohibition pin the artifact tightly, and the profile is explicit that difficulty is not drift risk. The main uncertainty is whether the container can run a two-rank process group at all — if it cannot, B5's self-measurement loop weakens toward 1.

rows.name: torch-tensor-parallelism

evidence.B1: "receive an initialized master_weight ... and split it across ranks so each rank gets its partition" then forward consumes that shard — a natural write-then-use order inside each class, but the two classes are independent and no separate step's artifact feeds another.
evidence.B3: metadata expertMinutes = 240 (4 hours), difficulty "hard" — squarely in the profile's 2–8 hour band, though agentTimeoutSec is only 900.
evidence.B5: Semantics are stated well enough to self-check — "concatenated along the last dimension as if using all_gather", "partial outputs should be summed together as if using all_reduce", "world_size values of 1, 2, and 4" — so the agent can build an unsharded nn.Linear reference and compare. That is a pass/fail equivalence check with no scale to improve along.
