evidence.B8: Output is pinned tightly: exact path "/app/parallel_linear.py", exact constructor signatures, sharding axis per class, "initialize the bias to zero", and the tested surface enumerated ("initialization and sharding of weights and bias, output results, and gradients"). Residual freedom is in derived details — grad handling for the full row-parallel bias, real vs. emulated collectives — so an error would still look well-formed.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes = 240 → 2–8 hour band: orchestration turns are material but do not dominate a half-day implementation.
evidence.C4: The method is conventional for the domain and largely spelled out ("splits the weight matrix by columns", "each rank's forward() receives only its pre-scattered slice of the input", "fetch the world_size and rank ... using torch.distributed.get_world_size()"); only the tooling choice — real collectives vs. emulated gather/reduce — is open.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/tdd.js + library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent writes both classes, validates only at world_size=1 (where sharding is a no-op and all_gather/all_reduce collapse to identity), and declares done — shipping a RowParallelLinear that adds the full bias once per rank instead of once into the summed output, or a ColumnParallelLinear whose bias shard is misaligned with its output shard. Both pass every check the agent actually ran and fail at world_size 2 and 4.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is horizon: a 240-minute expert estimate (B3=2) is the only live dimension carrying real weight; everything else scores 1. The output contract is unusually tight — exact file path, exact signatures, per-class sharding axis, zero bias init, and an explicit list of what is tested — so drift risk stays at 1 despite the "hard" difficulty label; difficulty is not drift. The method is textbook tensor parallelism described almost procedurally, giving C4=1, and at four hours the ceremony is noticeable but not dominant (C2=1). The counterfactual is concrete rather than vague: world_size=1 is a degenerate case in which every sharding and reduction bug disappears, so a vanilla agent can honestly believe it is finished while the 2- and 4-rank paths are wrong.

rows.name: train-fasttext

evidence.B1: "train a fasttext model on the yelp data in the data/ folder" ... "model size needs to be less than 150MB but get at least 0.62 accuracy" ... "saved as /app/model.bin" — the raw yelp data must be converted to fasttext's __label__ supervised format before training, and the trained model must then be size-reduced (quantization/dim reduction) before being written to the target path. Each step consumes the previous step's artifact, and doing size reduction before measuring accuracy inverts the check the constraints require.
evidence.B3: metadata: expertMinutes 30, agentTimeoutSec 3600. Against a corpus median of 120 expert-minutes this sits at the low end of the ~30-120 band; one sitting plus some training wall-clock, well inside a single context window.
evidence.B5: "needs to be less than 150MB but get at least 0.62 accuracy on a private test set that comes from the same yelp review distribution" — both quantities are locally computable by the agent (stat the model file; hold out a split of data/ and run fasttext's own test), and both come with an explicit figure to beat, so there is a defined finish line with headroom to iterate on hyperparameters and quantization.
evidence.B6: The deliverable is one artifact, /app/model.bin. The two constraints (size, accuracy) are jointly optimized over the same training run, not independent units that could fan out and be verified separately.
evidence.B8: "The model should be saved as /app/model.bin" plus two numeric constraints pin path, format and acceptance criteria exactly. The residual gap is that hyperparameters, preprocessing and quantization settings are the agent's to derive — a model that overfits a self-chosen validation split would still be a well-formed .bin at the right path.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 30 with agentTimeoutSec 3600 — a preprocess/train/quantize/verify loop measured in tens of minutes. Mandatory per-step stops and journaling would be a noticeable fraction of a task this size.
evidence.C4: "the yelp data in the data/ folder" — the supplied dataset must be inspected before the method can be fixed: its format (CSV vs. raw text, star ratings vs. binary polarity, label column layout) determines the preprocessing and the label mapping, and its size determines whether quantization alone or dim/bucket reduction is needed to stay under 150MB. The training method itself is conventional for fasttext, but the procedure cannot be chosen until the input is read.

rows.processRecommendation: library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js composed with an iterative-convergence loop (gate: held-out accuracy >= 0.62 AND stat -c%s /app/model.bin < 150MB, re-checked after quantization)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The likely vanilla failure is skipping local measurement of the two stated constraints: the agent runs `fasttext supervised` with defaults on the whole of data/, never carves out a held-out split, and declares done on train-set accuracy — or it hits 0.62 with a full-precision model of several hundred MB, then runs `quantize` to get under 150MB and never re-evaluates accuracy after quantization. Either way a well-formed /app/model.bin exists and the agent reports success, while the private test comes back under 0.62.
rows.rationale: The decisive live factor is B5=3: the instruction states two figures the agent can compute for itself before the verifier ever runs — file size and held-out accuracy — which is exactly the shape a scored convergence loop exploits, and the concrete vanilla failure (quantize, then never re-measure) is the loop's whole point. Against that, both cost dimensions land mid-scale: at 30 expert-minutes the per-step ceremony is a real fraction of the work (C2=2), and the method cannot be pinned until the data/ folder is inspected for label format and corpus size (C4=2). B1=2 for the format-to-train-to-compress chain, but the pipeline is conventional enough that an agent is unlikely to invert it. B3=1 and B6=0 contribute little: one sitting, one indivisible artifact. Benefit_live 48.9 against Cost_live 66.7 gives net_live -17.8; net_raw is 61.7 - 71.0 = -9.3.

rows.name: tune-mjcf

evidence.B1: "The /app/eval.py script can help you iterate" plus "The initial model is at /app/model_ref.xml and should remain unchanged. Tuned mjcf should be saved as /app/model.xml." There is a natural reading order — measure the reference baseline, edit, re-measure — but nothing downstream silently breaks if you deviate, since eval.py recomputes the comparison on each run.
evidence.B3: metadata: expertMinutes 30, difficulty "medium", agentTimeoutSec 900 (15 minutes). A single focused sitting, far under the corpus median of 120 expert-minutes; no distinct phases, one file to produce.
evidence.B5: "takes 60% of the original time or less" and "The same full physics state should be reached within atol=1e-5 without NaN or Inf", with "The /app/eval.py script can help you iterate" — a self-measurable quantity plus an explicitly stated figure to beat and a supplied measuring tool.
evidence.B6: One deliverable: "Tuned mjcf should be saved as /app/model.xml." A single XML file whose numerical settings interact; no independent units that could fan out in parallel.
evidence.B8: Output path, format and acceptance criteria are pinned ("/app/model.xml", 60% of original time, atol=1e-5, no NaN/Inf, model_ref.xml unchanged), and the instruction pre-empts the main wrong turns: "hint: changing physical properties of the bodies will break them" and "There is no need to look for plugins". The agent still derives which numerical options to change, so a bad edit would still read as a well-formed mjcf.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 30 and agentTimeoutSec 900 — a sub-30-minute edit of one XML file; mandatory per-step stops and journaling would cost more turns than the tuning itself.
evidence.C4: The instruction names the supplied input ("The initial model is at /app/model_ref.xml") but not the procedure: which of timestep, solver, iterations, integrator or collision settings can be loosened without moving the physics state depends entirely on what that model contains, so the method can only be chosen after inspecting it.

rows.processRecommendation: library/specializations/performance-optimization/ composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gate: python /app/eval.py) and library/processes/shared/n-strikes-escalation.js
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent optimizes for the timing target alone — enlarging the timestep or cutting solver iterations — confirms the run is under 60% of baseline, and declares done without re-verifying that the final physics state still matches within atol=1e-5 and is free of NaN/Inf; or it trims body masses/geoms for speed despite the hint, shipping a model.xml that is fast and plausible-looking but fails the correctness test.
rows.rationale: Cost dominates decisively: a 30-expert-minute task with a 900s agent timeout, producing a single XML file (C2=3), where the method only becomes clear after reading model_ref.xml (C4=2), leaves orchestration overhead larger than the work. The one strong benefit is B5=3 — "60% of the original time or less" plus atol=1e-5 and a supplied eval.py give a genuine scored iterate-until-target loop with a defined finish line — but that loop is equally available to a vanilla agent invoking eval.py in a shell. B1, B3 and B6 sit at or near zero: one file, one sitting, no fan-out, no step consuming an earlier step's artifact. Drift risk is low because the instruction pins the path, the tolerances, and even the two main wrong turns. The concrete vanilla failure — hitting the speed target while skipping the state-match/NaN check — is real, but a single eval.py run catches it, so it does not carry the routing.

rows.name: video-processing

evidence.B1: "You can assume the first frame of the video has no runner on the track" plus "You have to figure out how to detect when the jump happens" implies a chained pipeline inside one deliverable: build a background model from frame 0 -> subtract to get per-frame foreground/athlete position -> derive a trajectory -> read takeoff and landing frames off that trajectory. Each step consumes the previous step's derived value, so the wrong order silently yields plausible-but-wrong frame numbers. Not 3 because the instruction never states the procedure; the ordering is inherent to a method the agent chooses rather than an explicit first-X-then-Y-then-Z contract.
evidence.B3: metadata: "expertMinutes": 400 (~6.7 hours), "difficulty": "hard" - inside the ~2-8 hour band. "agentTimeoutSec": 3600 is below the 7200 anchor, so 2 rather than 3.
evidence.B5: "There's an example video for development in `/app/example_video.mp4`" and "In the video, there is a single jump recorded" - the agent can run its detector on a supplied input and decode frames to check whether it found the jump at all. That is a pass/fail sanity check with no scale: no labelled takeoff/land frames, no error metric, and no tolerance figure is given, so the agent cannot compute a quantity and tell whether it improved.
evidence.B6: Single indivisible deliverable - one script at `/app/jump_analyzer.py` producing one file `/app/output.toml`. The two fields (`jump_takeoff_frame_number`, `jump_land_frame_number`) come off the same motion trajectory and cannot be worked independently. No fan-out of files, cases, or targets.
evidence.B8: The contract is pinned hard: exact script path `/app/jump_analyzer.py`, exact output path `/app/output.toml`, "exactly these fields and names", two integers, and a closed dependency list ("You can only use these libraries": toml, cv2 and numpy). What is not pinned is the numeric content - "You have to figure out how to detect when the jump happens" means a mis-detected takeoff frame still emits a perfectly well-formed TOML that reads as complete. Format pinned, content derived -> 1.
evidence.C2: "expertMinutes": 400 (~6.7 hours) places this in the ~2-8 hour band: mandatory per-step stops are material but do not dominate a task of this size. Scored consistently with B3=2.
evidence.C4: The instruction leads with a goal, not a symptom, so the 3-line does not fire. But "You have to figure out how to detect when the jump happens" and "There's an example video for development in `/app/example_video.mp4`" mean the method - background subtraction vs. optical flow vs. contour/centroid tracking, and what signal marks takeoff - cannot be chosen until the supplied video is inspected for framing, contrast, athlete size, and frame rate. Naming `/app/output.toml` and the field names does not reduce this; the artifacts are specified, the procedure is not.

rows.processRecommendation: custom
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent tunes its detector against the one supplied `/app/example_video.mp4` - hard-coding a pixel row for the ground line, a foreground-area threshold, or in the worst case the frame numbers themselves - sees a plausible pair of integers in `/app/output.toml`, and declares done. Because "All test videos will have the same dimensions and scale as the example provided" but not the same athlete or timing, the script emits well-formed but wrong frame numbers on `test_video.mp4`, and nothing in a vanilla session forces the agent to separate "detector generalizes" from "numbers look right on the example" before stopping.
rows.rationale: Cost edges out benefit here. The dominant cost is C4=2: the instruction pins the artifacts precisely but not the method, and the detection approach only becomes choosable after inspecting the example video, so any process encoded up front is partly a guess. On the benefit side B1=2 and B3=2 carry the weight - a genuinely chained background-model -> trajectory -> event-detection pipeline at ~400 expert-minutes - but B6=0 (one script, one output) and B8=1 (exact path, exact field names, closed library list) give orchestration little to protect. B5=1 is the pivotal limiter: there is an example video to run against but no labels, tolerance, or error metric, so a convergence loop has no scale to iterate on and would degrade into the agent asserting its own detections look right. The counterfactual is concrete and real - overfitting to the single example and declaring success - but it argues for one verification gate, not for a full governed run.

rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent runs `strings` on the binary, finds a plausible decoy or a truncated `FLAG{`-prefixed literal, and writes it to /app/results.txt without ever making the program actually emit the secret — the file is well-formed and the agent declares success on a wrong value. rows.name: write-compressor

evidence.B1: "I have a decompressor in /app/decomp.c... Write me data.comp that's compressed such that running cat data.comp | /app/decomp gives exactly data.txt" — the bit/byte-level format must first be derived from decomp.c, and that derived format is the input to the encoder that produces data.comp; encode before (or without) fully deriving the format and the artifact is silently wrong-but-plausible. One chained dependency inside a single deliverable, not two.
evidence.B3: metadata expertMinutes: 1440 (24 hours), difficulty: "hard" — over the profile's ~8-hour line for B3=3, well above the corpus median of 120.
evidence.B5: The agent can compute both feedback signals itself: correctness via `cat data.comp | /app/decomp` diffed against /app/data.txt, and size against the stated ceiling "data.comp must be at most 2500 bytes" — a measurable quantity with an explicit figure to beat and headroom to iterate on.
evidence.B6: Single indivisible deliverable: one file, data.comp, produced by one encoder derived from one decompressor source. No independent units named in the instruction that could be verified alone.
evidence.B8: Output is pinned exactly: a named file whose content is fixed by byte-identical round-trip equality ("gives exactly data.txt") plus a hard size bound. "You can generate data.comp any way you want" leaves method free but not the artifact — a wrong answer fails the diff visibly.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes: 1440 — at ~24 hours of expert work, per-step mandatory stops are a rounding error against the work itself.
evidence.C4: "I have a decompressor in /app/decomp.c" — the encoding procedure cannot be chosen until that supplied source is read and its format reverse-engineered; also depends on inspecting /app/data.txt's redundancy to hit 2500 bytes. Not a symptom-led diagnosis task, so it stops at the 2 line.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/tdd.js composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gate: `cat /app/data.comp | /app/decomp | diff - /app/data.txt` and a `wc -c /app/data.comp` size assertion), with an iterative-convergence loop driving the byte count under 2500
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent skims decomp.c, assumes a familiar scheme instead of decoding its exact bit order and end-of-stream handling, and ships a data.comp that diverges from data.txt partway through (or exceeds 2500 bytes), declaring success without running `cat data.comp | /app/decomp | diff - /app/data.txt` and `wc -c data.comp`.
rows.rationale: Horizon dominates the benefit side: 1440 expert-minutes on a "hard" task puts this well past a single sitting, and the same figure zeroes C2, so orchestration overhead is essentially free here. B5 is a genuine 3 rather than a pin artifact — the agent owns both feedback signals locally (byte-exact round-trip through /app/decomp, and file size against the explicitly stated 2500-byte ceiling), which is precisely the shape a convergence loop with a real finish line needs. Working against that, B8 is 0 and B6 is 0: the deliverable is one file with an exact output contract, so difficulty here is not drift — a confidently wrong answer is visibly wrong on the first diff. rows.name: atrx-vep-crispr

evidence.B1: Explicit chained pipeline where each stage consumes the previous one's output: reconstruct the WT transcript from `/app/data/genomic-locus.fa` + `CDS-information.txt`, then 'Catalogue all coding variants ... relative to the wild-type NM_000489.6 reference', then 'Annotate the coding variants that you find using the resource at /app/data/ensembl-vep-release-115/', then 'identify the NMD-escaping variant whose VEP-predicted amino acid position overlaps with this Pfam domain', then 'Map the chosen NMD-escaping variant back to its 1-based forward-strand reference position', then 'Identify the target site for canonical SpCas9 in the derived mutant genomic DNA sequence'. A wrong CDS reconstruction or variant set silently propagates into a plausible-but-wrong guide RNA.
evidence.B3: `expertMinutes: 420` (7 hours) and `agentTimeoutSec: 18000`, well above the profile's 7200 bar for a 2; several distinct phases (transcript reconstruction, variant calling, offline VEP run, InterPro domain lookup, genomic mapping, CRISPR target search) but under the ~8-hour bar for 3.
evidence.B5: The agent can self-check without the hidden verifier: variants called 'relative to the wild-type NM_000489.6 reference' can be re-applied to the reconstructed WT transcript and compared against `/app/data/mutated-transcripts.txt`, and the guide must have a 'PAM sequence matching the NGG pattern' checkable against the derived sequence. These are pass/fail checks with no scale, target figure, or quantity to iterate toward.
evidence.B6: Limited fan-out: 'a list of mutated transcript sequences' implies per-transcript variant calling, and the Pfam lookup in `/app/data/InterPro-domain-information.tsv` is independent of the VEP run, but the deliverable is a single `/app/output/mutation.report.json` whose `selected_variant`, `mutant_genomic_dna_fragment` and `spcas9_target` fields are strictly serial.
evidence.B8: The output is pinned: one path (`/app/output/mutation.report.json`), a literal JSON schema naming every field and convention ('1-based GRCh38 forward-strand coordinate (VCF normalisation for indels)', '20-nt ACGT string of the protospacer'), plus an explicit tie-break ('select the SpCas9 target site that has the lower genomic coordinate of its cut site'). Content is agent-derived so errors look well-formed, but two competent agents cannot produce materially different-shaped artifacts.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 420` with an 18000-second agent budget puts this in the profile's ~2-8 hour band: per-step orchestration stops are material but do not dominate a multi-hour bioinformatics pipeline.
evidence.C4: The instruction enumerates the procedure in order and names the tooling ('Annotate ... using the resource at /app/data/ensembl-vep-release-115/ in offline mode', 'Use the /app/data/InterPro-domain-information.tsv table', 'canonical SpCas9', 'canonical HGVS (c.) transcript-level notation'). No diagnosis is required and no supplied input must be inspected before the method can be chosen; only tooling details (VEP invocation flags, the bundled NMD plugin, alignment method for variant calling) are open.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/plan-and-execute.js composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (per-stage gate: WT transcript round-trip against mutated-transcripts.txt, VEP invocation exit code, final JSON schema validation); no genomics specialization exists, so the stage definitions are custom.
rows.vanillaFailureMode: A vanilla agent skips the offline VEP run — hand-deriving consequence terms and the NMD-escape flag from the 50-nt-rule of thumb instead of the NM_000489.6-specific annotations the instruction demands — and picks the last-listed row of `InterPro-domain-information.tsv` as the 'most C-terminally positioned Pfam domain' without filtering to Pfam entries or sorting by residue end. Either error silently selects the wrong variant, and because every later field (`selected_variant`, `genomic_coordinate`, `mutant_genomic_dna_fragment`, `spcas9_target`) is derived from that choice, the agent writes a fully schema-valid JSON and declares success while nearly all computed fields are wrong.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is B1: this is a six-stage dependency chain in which the output of each stage is the input to the next, and an error at any upstream stage (CDS reconstruction, HGVS variant calling, VEP consequence/NMD assignment, Pfam domain selection) propagates silently into a schema-valid final report — exactly the failure enforcement of ordering and per-stage gates is meant to catch. B3=2 is supported by 420 expert-minutes and an 18000-second agent timeout, both above the profile's bar. Costs stay low: the procedure is stated step by step with the tooling named (C4=1), and a multi-hour task absorbs orchestration turns easily (C2=1). B5, B6 and B8 are all 1 — the agent has only pass/fail self-checks, the artifact is a single serial JSON, and the output contract is pinned field by field, so difficulty here is not drift risk. Live scores land clearly on the benefit side, driven by ordering and horizon rather than by the task merely being hard.

rows.name: batched-eval-parity

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/tdd.js composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (parity sweep over batch-size x padding-side x batch-mode x cold/warm cache as the gate command); library/specializations/qa-testing-automation/ is the nearest domain fit.

rows.name: biped-contact-dynamics

evidence.B1: The deliverable is one script but its internals form a chained derivation: "state has shape (K, 14) and stores Drake positions followed by velocities" and "velocities must integrate to positions with a trapezoidal residual below 0.005" — positions must be produced before consistent velocities; then "both the floating-base and full inverse-dynamics residuals must remain below 30" and "contact forces ... must be consistent with the full multibody dynamics" means torques and contact forces must be derived from those same states/accelerations. A mode schedule must also be fixed first ("Modes must strictly alternate LEFT_STANCE -> FLIGHT -> RIGHT_STANCE") because contact forces are only admissible per mode. Two or more dependencies chained; computing torques from a trajectory whose velocities were later re-smoothed silently yields plausible-but-inconsistent arrays.
evidence.B3: metadata expertMinutes = 300 (5 hours, in the ~2-8h band) and agentTimeoutSec = 14400, well above the 7200 threshold; the instruction itself states "You have 14400 seconds to complete this task" and each generator invocation may take up to 1200 seconds, so tuning cycles are long.
evidence.B5: Every acceptance signal is a quantity the agent can compute locally with PyDrake and a stated figure to beat: "trapezoidal residual below 0.005", "center-of-mass force-balance residual must remain below 100 N", "floating-base and full inverse-dynamics residuals must remain below 30", "contact-force rate must remain below 8000 N/s", "actuator-torque rate must remain below 3500 N-m/s", "more than 0.12 m of clearance", "6 cm or more", "10th percentile of base x-velocity must stay above 40% of its mean". The verifier's aggregation is also described ("excludes the first and last 3 samples and a margin of 5 samples ... 95th-percentile checks"), so the agent can replicate the metric and iterate toward the target.
evidence.B6: Three separately-verified artifacts — "/app/results/walk.npz, /app/results/jump.npz, and /app/results/run.npz" — each with its own mode and clearance requirements, but they must all be produced by one entrypoint ("python /app/submission/solve.py --config CONFIG_JSON --output OUTPUT_DIR") and share one model, one dynamics/inverse-dynamics core and one set of residual tolerances, so fan-out buys little.
evidence.B8: The output contract is pinned to the byte: exact paths, "arrays named t, state, u, contact_forces, and mode", shapes (K,), (K,14), (K,4), actuator order "[left hip, right hip, left knee, right knee]", contact order "left horizontal, left vertical, right horizontal, right vertical", mode codes 0-3, torque bound +/-500, and numeric residual ceilings. The long constraint list narrows the gap; residual freedom is only in derived content — a submission can be well-formed (right shapes, right mode sequence) while the inverse-dynamics residuals are wrong, which is the anti-drift-detectable failure the instruction pre-empts with "The dynamics requirement is full multibody consistency, not only center-of-mass force balance."
evidence.C2: expertMinutes = 300 (5 hours) sits in the ~2-8 hour band; with a 14400 s agent budget and 1200 s per generator run, mandatory per-step stops are material but do not dominate the work.
evidence.C4: The instruction leads with an implementation goal, not a symptom, so it is not a 3 — but the procedure cannot be chosen until supplied inputs are inspected: "A non-functional starter script /app/make_trajectories.py is provided to illustrate the expected output schema", the model referenced via "use the model_path specified there" (planar_walker.urdf), and "The notes in /app/README_2DBiped.md summarize the model coordinates, actuator/contact ordering, and useful PyDrake dynamics APIs." The method is also explicitly left open: "The chosen solution method (closed-form inverse dynamics, trajectory optimization, RL, etc.) is not constrained".

rows.processRecommendation: library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js composed under library/methodologies/plan-and-execute.js (self-computed residual gates per gait: trapezoidal integration, full inverse dynamics, contact/torque rates, mode-sequence check, plus a rerun gate over synthetic alternate configs)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent gets a kinematically pretty gait that satisfies the visible config and the easy checks (mode ordering, foot clearance, COM force balance) and declares success without ever computing the full multibody inverse-dynamics residual per sample — the instruction warns precisely about this ("The dynamics requirement is full multibody consistency, not only center-of-mass force balance") — so walk/jump/run.npz are well-formed, correctly shaped, and silently fail the 30-residual and 3500 N-m/s torque-rate gates. The second concrete failure is scope truncation at the end of a long session: the generator is tuned against /app/configs/visible.json only and never re-run against a modified step length / jump height, so the hidden-config reruns produce trajectories that miss the distance or height target.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is B1: although there is a single script deliverable, its internals are a chained derivation — mode schedule, then positions, then velocities consistent with those positions under a trapezoidal residual of 0.005, then torques and contact forces consistent with the full multibody dynamics — and getting that order wrong produces arrays that look correct and fail numerically. B5 is also maximal because every acceptance criterion is a number the agent can compute itself with PyDrake (0.005, 100 N, 30, 8000 N/s, 3500 N-m/s, 0.12 m, 6 cm, 40% of mean), so an iterate-until-target loop is available without the hidden verifier. B3 is 2 on 300 expert-minutes and a 14400 s agent timeout, which also holds C2 down to 1. The main cost is C4=2: the method is explicitly unconstrained and the procedure only becomes choosable after inspecting the URDF, the README coordinate/ordering notes, and the non-functional starter script. B8 is low despite the difficulty, because the output contract pins paths, array names, shapes, orderings and bounds exactly — difficulty is not drift risk.

rows.name: bun-sourcemap-leak

evidence.B1: Real data dependencies in the pipeline: 'Use /app/visibility.json as the provenance policy' must be read before redaction decisions; the map must be emitted as an external file at /app/dist/client-entry.js.map and then have its `sources` rewritten to 'resolve relative to the emitted .map file location'; and the manifest at /app/dist/release-manifest.json must list shipped artifacts and 'any provenance it describes must be public', which consumes the redacted map. Generating the manifest before redaction silently ships leaky provenance. Not 3: the requirements are a checklist, not an explicit first-X-then-Y-then-Z, and only one or two hops are load-bearing.
evidence.B3: metadata expertMinutes: 90 and agentTimeoutSec: 1800 — squarely in the ~30–120 minute band; a single sitting, no resume expected.
evidence.B5: Self-checkable worked examples exist: client must 'print the public client greeting exactly as `Hello, Ada!`', server must print 'PUBLIC_RESPONSE: Hello, Ada!', and the '--trace-probe path must still report PUBLIC_RENDER_PROBE and resolve to src/client/render.ts'. The agent can also grep /app/dist against privateSources. All pass/fail with no scale or target to iterate toward.
evidence.B6: Three loosely separable parts — client bundle plus external map redaction, the server artifact that 'only needs to preserve the required public server response', and release-manifest.json — but all are emitted by the one `bun run release` pipeline and share the visibility.json policy read. One artifact with parts, not genuine fan-out.
evidence.B8: Most outputs are pinned exactly (paths /app/dist/client-entry.js.map and /app/dist/release-manifest.json, the literal replacement `[private]`, exact stdout strings), which constrains tightly. The gap is two outcome-shaped clauses: 'uses the client source tree and provenance policy of whatever input app is present in /app at runtime' and 'No shipped artifact under /app/dist may expose ... private module identities, private source names, or local filesystem paths.' Two competent agents could ship materially different pipelines — one generic and policy-driven, one special-cased to the app currently in /app — both looking complete.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes: 90 → the ~30–120 minute band, where per-step mandatory stops are a noticeable fraction of the work; the whole agent budget is agentTimeoutSec: 1800.
evidence.C4: Symptom-first framing: 'Fix the Bun/TypeScript app's production release pipeline, which currently leaks private source provenance through generated artifacts.' The first real step is diagnosing the existing release script and how Bun emits sources/sourcesContent. Naming the output files does not make the method known — the earlier ladder line wins.

rows.processRecommendation: library/specializations/security-compliance/ combined with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js and forbidden-markers-scanner.js for leak scanning over /app/dist; no exact library process for build/source-map provenance redaction, so otherwise custom.
rows.vanillaFailureMode: A vanilla agent hardcodes redaction to the private files of the app currently in /app, sees the two exact greetings print, and declares done — so the pipeline fails on a swapped variant app despite the 'whatever input app is present in /app at runtime' requirement; and it leaves an inline or `sourceRoot`-based client map whose `sources` do not resolve relative to the emitted .map file, which still deobfuscates under a casual local check.
rows.rationale: Cost dominates. The instruction is symptom-led — the pipeline 'currently leaks private source provenance' — so diagnosis of the existing build and of Bun's source-map emission must precede any encodable plan, pinning C4 at 3, and at 90 expert minutes the orchestration ceremony is a material fraction of the work (C2=2). The strongest benefit signal is B1: policy read → bundle → external-map redaction → manifest is a genuine dependency chain in which manifest-before-redaction silently ships leaky provenance. B8 is 2 rather than higher because paths, the literal `[private]` marker, and exact stdout strings are all pinned; the residual gap is the runtime-generalization clause, which is exactly where a vanilla run most plausibly declares premature success. Horizon and decomposability are both low — one sitting, one pipeline — so neither journaling nor fan-out earns anything here.

rows.name: cad-model

evidence.B1: "output a STEP file in /app/out.step which contains the object described by the 2d schematic in /app/schematic.png" — the dimensions and features must first be extracted from the image, and those derived values are then consumed by the modeling script; within the model, construction order (profile sketch -> extrude/revolve -> secondary features such as holes/fillets -> export) is itself dependency-ordered, so a wrong order yields a geometrically wrong but still exportable solid. One clear chain, not two independent ones.
evidence.B3: metadata: "agentTimeoutSec": 7200 (profile: at/above 7200 -> 2) and "expertMinutes": 120, i.e. the corpus median; a multi-hour CAD modeling session.
evidence.B5: The supplied "/app/schematic.png" is a reference the agent can check itself against — it can re-render or query its own model and see whether it matches the drawing. But the instruction states no figure to beat and no error metric; the check is essentially pass/fail against the picture, with no scale of improvement.
evidence.B6: A single indivisible deliverable: one STEP file at one path describing one object. No independent units to fan out; nothing in the instruction names multiple parts, cases or targets.
evidence.B8: Output is pinned by path and format ("a STEP file in /app/out.step") and the content is fully determined by the supplied schematic, so the goal is not open-ended. Residual risk is only that a dimension or feature read off the image is wrong — the file would still be a well-formed STEP solid, i.e. an error that looks correct.
evidence.C2: "expertMinutes": 120 sits in the ~30-120 minute band; against roughly two hours of modeling work, mandatory per-step stops and journaling are a noticeable fraction of the total, though not dominant.
evidence.C4: The procedure cannot be chosen until the supplied input is inspected: the instruction only says the object is "described by the 2d schematic in /app/schematic.png". Whether the part is an extrusion, a revolve, or a multi-feature body — and hence the entire modeling approach — is unknowable until the image is read. It does not lead with a symptom or complaint, so not 3.

rows.processRecommendation: custom
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent reads the schematic once, misreads or silently drops a dimension/feature (a hole diameter, a chamfer, a hidden-line view it never reconciled), writes a syntactically valid STEP body, and declares success without ever re-rendering the solid and comparing it view-by-view against schematic.png — producing a file that opens cleanly in any CAD viewer but is the wrong part.
rows.rationale: Cost dominates a modest benefit. The single deliverable is exactly pinned — one STEP file at one path, geometry fully determined by a supplied drawing — so drift risk is low (B8=1) and there is nothing to decompose (B6=0). The real benefit is horizon: a 7200s agent timeout and 120 expert-minutes make this a long single artifact (B3=2), with a genuine construction-order chain from image-derived dimensions into the model (B1=2). Against that, the method is undiscoverable until the schematic is inspected (C4=2) — any process encoded up front would be guessing at extrude vs. revolve vs. multi-feature — and two hours of work makes per-step orchestration a noticeable overhead (C2=2). The counterfactual is concrete: the likely vanilla failure is a well-formed STEP file of the wrong part, shipped without a render-and-compare check against the drawing.

rows.name: cargo-flight-dispatch

evidence.B1: The instruction lays out a three-layer computation chain whose values feed forward: `/app/navigation.py` — distance, bearing, heading, wind triangle, and crosswind calculations`, then `/app/aircraft.py` — airspeed, fuel burn, weight, and reserve computations`, then `/app/dispatch.py` — route optimization, flight plan assembly`. True bearing feeds the wind triangle, which feeds groundspeed, which feeds leg time, which feeds fuel burn and reserves, which feed the feasibility of the tour ('Some island strips have no refueling capability — fuel planning for those legs is safety-critical'). Two or more dependencies chained: fixing route optimization or fuel while an upstream navigation value is still wrong silently yields a plausible-but-wrong plan.
evidence.B3: `expertMinutes: 150` — 2.5 hours, above the corpus median of 120 and inside the 2–8 hour band. `agentTimeoutSec: 3600` is below the 7200 marker, so 2 rather than 3.
evidence.B5: The agent can compute quantities itself and see whether they improved: 'fuel estimates that don't match their manual calculations' can be recomputed by hand-checking great-circle distance and wind-triangle groundspeed; the tour requirement 'depart NAN, visit every destination exactly once, and return to NAN' gives a total-distance/fuel objective the agent can score and reduce; 'must be deterministic — same inputs produce the same plan every run' is self-checkable by running twice. No stated target figure or baseline to beat, so 2 not 3.
evidence.B6: Three named modules (`navigation.py`, `aircraft.py`, `dispatch.py`) give some separable bug classes (crosswind vs. weight limits vs. route optimization), but they compose into one artifact — a single `/output/flight_plan.json` — and the downstream modules consume the upstream fixes, so they are not independently verifiable units. Modest fan-out only.
evidence.B8: The bug set is unenumerated and described in outcome terms: 'there are bugs ranging from missing features that the data files support but the code ignores to incorrect computations' and 'produces a correct flight plan'. The output path is pinned but its content is entirely agent-derived, so an agent that fixes four of the defects and stops emits a well-formed, confident, wrong plan. Two competent agents could plausibly ship materially different plans (different tour order, different fuel figures) that both satisfy the stated text. Constraints such as the exact-once tour, no mid-route hub return, and determinism narrow the gap below 3.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 150` — 2.5 hours of expert work. Orchestration turns are material but do not dominate a multi-module debugging effort; scored consistently with B3=2.
evidence.C4: The instruction leads with a symptom, not a procedure: 'has been producing incorrect results since the last software update. Pilots report fuel estimates that don't match their manual calculations, weights that cleared loads they know were over limit, and crosswind limits being ignored on approach.' It then says 'Read the code and the data files carefully' — the first real step is diagnosis of an unknown defect set. Naming the three source files and the four data files does not cancel this; the earliest matching ladder line wins.

rows.processRecommendation: library/cradle/bugfix.js composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (diagnose-inventory-defects → fix-navigation → fix-aircraft → fix-dispatch, each gated on `python /app/dispatch.py --output /output/flight_plan.json` exiting 0 plus a repeat-run byte-identical determinism check)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent fixes the loudest, most visible defects — great-circle distance and per-leg fuel burn — sees a well-formed `/output/flight_plan.json` appear, and declares success while silently leaving the "missing features that the data files support but the code ignores" unimplemented: magnetic declination never applied to convert true bearings to magnetic headings, antimeridian-crossing legs computed with a wrong longitude delta, and the crosswind component never checked against the Caravan's limit using runway headings. The resulting plan is plausible and internally consistent, so nothing in the agent's own view flags it, and the no-refuel legs get fuel figures that are quietly unsafe.
rows.rationale: The decisive tension is a deep forward-dependent computation chain (navigation → aircraft → dispatch, where a wrong bearing corrupts groundspeed, fuel, and ultimately the tour choice) pulling toward enforcement, against a task that opens with a complaint rather than a procedure and so demands diagnosis before any process could be encoded. B1=3 and B8=2 give a real payoff for staged, gated fixing with a premature-'done' guard, and B5=2 because the agent can self-measure tour cost, determinism, and hand-checked distances. But C4=3 fires on the first ladder line — 'producing incorrect results since the last software update... Pilots report' — and naming the six files does not cancel it, while 150 expert-minutes keeps C2 at 1 rather than 0. The counterfactual is concrete and not empty: the likeliest vanilla outcome is a well-formed plan that silently omits magnetic declination, antimeridian handling, and the crosswind check. Net is close to even; the orchestrator will place it from net_live.

rows.name: cli-2ph-simplex

evidence.B1: A chained pipeline is mandated: parse input -> build Phase 1 tableau -> "--initial_pivots ... apply them immediately after constructing the Phase 1 tableau" -> continue Phase 1 pivots -> "Artificial variable columns are removed at the end of Phase 1" -> Phase 2 -> and only then the derived artifacts: "in the final tableau, the problem is degenerate if any constraint row ... has an RHS of 0 within 1e-9" and "one valid final basis represented by the final tableau and the corresponding tableau RHS values". Section 10 further orders side effects after success: "If any exception is raised during execution, the implementation must not create the output file...". Two or more dependencies chained; wrong order (dropping artificial columns before Phase 1 ends, or applying the prefix pivots after canonicalization) silently yields a plausible-but-wrong tableau.
evidence.B3: expertMinutes: 120 and agentTimeoutSec: 2500 (~42 min), well below the 7200s bar for a 2; single container, single deliverable CLI. Sits at the top of the ~30-120 minute band.
evidence.B5: "choose subsequent pivots so that the total number of pivot-log entries, including the provided prefix pivots, is the smallest possible among all valid paths" - pivot count is a quantity the agent can compute for its own runs and tell whether it decreased. The instruction also supplies a worked invocation form the agent can run end-to-end. No target figure is handed to the agent, so not a 3.
evidence.B6: Starter modules are named (/app/simplex/parser.py, phases.py, schema.py, tableau.py) and the problem report is defined purely over the parsed input ("must represent that parsed input, not the solved output"), so the formatter is separable from the solver - but the tableau, pivot log, degeneracy report and basic-variable report all derive from one solver pipeline. Two loosely independent units, not fan-out.
evidence.B8: Output is pinned to the byte: exact CLI flags, "exact schema {\"step\": int, \"phase\": int, \"enter_column\": str, \"leave_row\": str, \"tableau\": list[list[float]]}", "exact signature {\"degenerate\": bool}", fixed column order with Z at index 0 and RHS last, half-up rounding to 2 decimals, and explicit sign/ordering rules for report terms. Residual freedom is only in derived content - "ties may be chosen freely", "report exactly one of them for that row" - so an arithmetic or pivot-selection error would still look well-formed.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes: 120, agentTimeoutSec: 2500 - squarely in the ~30-120 minute band where mandatory per-step stops are a noticeable fraction of the work.
evidence.C4: The instruction states the method rather than leading with a symptom: "slack for <=, surplus plus artificial for >=, and artificial only for =. Artificial variable columns are removed at the end of Phase 1", plus the exact validity condition for a pivot (negative reduced cost, minimum ratio). The only open choice is how to search for the minimum-length pivot path, since "Bland's rule, Dantzig's rule, or any other fixed pivot rule is not guaranteed to produce that required smallest total number of pivots" - a conventional algorithmic choice within a known domain, not an unknown shape.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/tdd.js composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent implements a standard Dantzig/Bland two-phase simplex, sees an optimal final tableau, and declares success - silently violating "the total number of pivot-log entries ... is the smallest possible among all valid paths", which no local check flags. The same premature-done pattern hits the low-salience clauses stated late in the instruction: writing the problem report from the standardized/solved form instead of "that parsed input, not the solved output", and creating output files before the run can raise, breaking "must not create the output file ... and must not create the pivot log file when requested".
rows.rationale: The decisive benefit is B1: this is a genuinely chained computation - Phase 1 construction, a mandated prefix of pivots applied at an exact point, artificial-column removal at the Phase 1 boundary, Phase 2, and only then the degeneracy and basic-variable reports read off the final tableau - where reordering yields a plausible but wrong artifact. Against that, the output contract is exhaustively specified, which suppresses drift risk (B8=1), and the work is a single indivisible solver, which suppresses decomposability (B6=1). Cost is dominated by C2: at 120 expert-minutes and a 2500s agent budget, per-step orchestration stops are a real fraction of the job, while C4 stays low because the algorithm itself is spelled out and only the minimum-pivot search is left open. The concrete vanilla failure is nameable - optimal-but-not-minimal pivot logs, plus the late-stated report-from-parsed-input and no-files-on-exception clauses getting dropped - so the counterfactual is not empty.

rows.name: coq-block-bound

evidence.B1: The instruction explicitly loosens ordering: "You may add auxiliary definitions and lemmas anywhere in the file or in new `.v` files in `/app/`." There is a natural reading order (inspect the abstract declarations of Triangle/path_valid/match_count, then build lemmas, then target_theorem), and Coq requires a lemma to precede its use, but a violation is a loud `coqc` compile error rather than a silently wrong result, and no intermediate artifact is consumed by a later independent step.
evidence.B3: `expertMinutes: 960` (16 hours) is well over the profile's ~8-hour line for 3, and `agentTimeoutSec: 14400` is double the 7200 threshold. Tags `imo`, `combinatorics`, `theorem-proving` describe work spanning many proof attempts, far beyond one context window.
evidence.B5: The instruction names a check the agent can run itself: "The build command `coqc -Q . Top Main.v` (run from `/app/`) must exit with code 0", plus grep-checkable negative constraints (no new `Axiom`, `Parameter`, `Conjecture`, `Admitted`, or `admit.`). This is pass/fail with no scale — no quantity to improve and no stated figure to beat, so 1 rather than 2.
evidence.B6: The deliverable is one theorem: "Prove `target_theorem` in `/app/Main.v`." Permission to "add auxiliary definitions and lemmas ... or in new `.v` files" allows some splitting into lemmas, but those lemmas are discovered while working the proof and all feed a single goal; they are not N independently verifiable units that could fan out in parallel.
evidence.B8: The output contract is tight: a named theorem in a named file, forbidden constructs enumerated ("must not introduce any new `Axiom`, `Parameter`, `Conjecture`, `Admitted`, or `admit.`"), forbidden edits enumerated ("must not modify the type signatures of ..."), and a single exit-code criterion. The proof body is agent-derived, so a semantically hollow-but-compiling artifact (a weakened auxiliary lemma, an undischarged hypothesis) would still look well-formed — hence 1 rather than 0. The gap for a confidently wrong yet instruction-satisfying answer is otherwise near zero.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 960` and `agentTimeoutSec: 14400`; against 16 expert-hours of proof search, mandatory per-step stops and journaling are a rounding error.
evidence.C4: The instruction names the artifacts exactly but not the method: the file "declares an abstract type `Triangle`, an abstract type `Path`, predicates `triangle_valid` and `path_valid`, a function `match_count`, an auxiliary function `log2_nat`" — the proof strategy cannot be chosen until `/app/Main.v` has been read and the actual definitions inspected. It does not lead with a symptom or a broken behaviour, so the 3 line does not match.

rows.processRecommendation: custom
rows.vanillaFailureMode: Four hours of single-session tactic exploration burns the context window; with the mathematical argument still unfinished, the agent takes the exit-code criterion literally and makes `coqc -Q . Top Main.v` return 0 by leaving a weakened auxiliary lemma that dodges the hard step (or by stating that step as a hypothesis it never discharges), then reports the theorem proved. Separately, with no journal, a restarted session re-walks induction schemes and bounds that were already tried and abandoned, because that record lived only in the lost context.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is horizon: 960 expert-minutes and a 14400-second agent timeout put this at the top of the corpus's B3 ladder, and the corresponding C2=0 means orchestration overhead is negligible against the work — a journal and resume are the concrete things vanilla lacks here. The counterfactual is concrete rather than generic: the stated success criterion is an exit code, so a context-exhausted agent has a plausible route to a compiling-but-hollow proof, and a lost session forfeits the record of failed proof strategies. Against that, the other live benefit dimensions are low: the instruction explicitly permits lemmas "anywhere in the file", so ordering is soft and misordering fails loudly (B1=1); the deliverable is one indivisible theorem (B6=1); and the output contract is pinned by name plus an explicit list of forbidden constructs, so difficulty here is not drift risk (B8=1). C4=2 because the proof strategy is discoverable only after reading the abstract definitions in the supplied file, not because the outputs are unnamed.

rows.name: ctr-optimization

evidence.B1: Hard temporal chain: the raw event log must be inspected and human/non-human traffic separated before any genuine-CTR estimate exists; that estimate drives parameter choice; each change 'incurs a 15min dead period (in simulated hours) while the new params take effect'; the final config must be committed and settled before hour 42 because 'No config change can be made during the evaluation period; any attempt will result in immediate failure', all while keeping 'at least 38 hours of airtime across the 48 hour campaign'. Reordering (e.g. exploring after hour 42, or spending dead periods late) silently and irrecoverably corrupts the result.
evidence.B3: expertMinutes 288 (~4.8h) and agentTimeoutSec 18000, both above the profile's 7200 anchor for 2; the simulation itself forces ~17,280s of real elapsed time (48 hours x 360s) that cannot be compressed, so the run spans explore -> commit -> hold phases across many polling cycles. Not scored 3: 288 expert-minutes is inside the 2-8h band, not over 8h.
evidence.B5: The agent can compute the quantity itself from the API ('The impression stream the API exposes is the raw event log') and has a stated finish line: 'the genuine user click-through rate (CTR) averages at least 2.2% during the evaluation window from hour 42 through hour 48'. Measurable quantity plus a target figure with headroom, testable against live hours before the window opens.
evidence.B6: One campaign, one config, one outcome. The only separable strands are the fraud-detection filter over the event log and the parameter exploration ('fraud-detection', 'exploration-exploitation' tags), and they are coupled — the filter is what scores the exploration. No fan-out of independently verifiable units.
evidence.B8: The target is a pinned number, but 'genuine user' is defined only as 'the raw event log ... includes both human and non-human' — the agent supplies its own definition. Two competent agents would plausibly ship materially different filters and parameter sets, each confidently reporting >=2.2% on its own filtered view, with the raw-vs-genuine gap invisible until the verifier runs. Blast radius is bounded to one config, which keeps it off 3.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes 288 (~4.8h) puts this in the 2-8h band; with ~17,280s of forced simulated-clock waiting, mandatory per-step stops are material but do not dominate the work. Scored consistently with B3=2.
evidence.C4: No symptom-led diagnosis (the goal is stated positively), but the method cannot be chosen until supplied inputs are inspected: 'The OpenAPI spec is served at the server's /openapi.json path' and the impression stream 'is the raw event log ... including both human and non-human'. Which delivery parameters exist, and what separates human from bot events, are only knowable after reading the spec and the log.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/state-machine-orchestration.js (timed phases with a hard freeze after hour 42, plus an airtime-budget gate) — or custom if no library process models a simulated clock
rows.vanillaFailureMode: A vanilla session optimizes against the raw event-log CTR without ever building a defensible human/bot separation, sees the bot-inflated number clear 2.2%, and locks in a config whose genuine CTR is well under target. The second concrete failure is clock bookkeeping across a ~4.8-hour real-time run: with no journal of when each 15-minute dead period was spent, the agent either drops below the '38 hours of airtime' floor through repeated reconfigs or issues one more config change after hour 42, which the instruction says causes 'immediate failure'.
rows.rationale: The decisive live dimension is B1: this task has a genuinely irreversible ordering constraint — measure, then commit, then freeze — enforced by a simulated clock, where a config change after hour 42 is instant failure and dead periods are drawn from a finite 38-hour airtime budget, so a reordering is not recoverable within the run. B5 is also maximal: the agent can compute genuine CTR itself and has a stated 2.2% line to clear, which is exactly the scored-iteration shape convergence loops serve. Against that, C4=2 is the dominant cost — the parameter space and the bot signature are only discoverable by reading /openapi.json and the raw event log, so any process encoded up front would have to leave the method open. B3 sits at 2 on the profile's anchors (288 expert-minutes, timeout 18000s) rather than 3, and C2=1 is scored consistently with it. B6 is near-zero: one campaign, one config, no fan-out.

rows.name: cumulative-layout-shift

evidence.B1: "Eliminate cumulative layout shift from the website at `/app/barber-shop-site/`" implies a natural inspect-then-fix order (measure which elements shift, then neutralize them), but no step produces an intermediate artifact a later step consumes — a fix applied before full diagnosis is simply re-measured, not silently corrupted. The baseline the visual comparison uses is already shipped (`eval/baseline.json`), so the agent does not have to produce it in sequence.
evidence.B3: `expertMinutes: 360` (6 hours, well above the corpus median of 120) and `agentTimeoutSec: 10800` (above the 7200 threshold); the site spans six routes (`app/page.tsx`, `about`, `services`, `gallery`, `book`, `socials`) plus a second container (`barber-shop-data-backend`), tagged `multi-container`.
evidence.B5: "All pages should measure zero CLS" is a stated target with a defined finish line, and CLS is a quantity the agent can compute for itself — the repo ships an agent-browser skill (`barber-shop-site/.claude/skills/agent-browser/SKILL.md`) and a CLS harness (`eval/lib/cls.ts`, `eval/scripts/run-cls.ts`), so the agent can measure, fix, and re-measure improvement before the hidden verifier runs.
evidence.B6: Six independent routes each measurable alone (`app/about`, `app/services`, `app/gallery`, `app/book`, `app/socials`, `app/page.tsx`) and many independently shifting components (`components/promo-banner.tsx`, `announcement-banner.tsx`, `home/social-feed.tsx`, `gallery-grid.tsx`, `home/team-preview-loader.tsx`). Not full fan-out, since shared roots — `app/layout.tsx`, the fonts under `public/fonts/`, and the third-party `public/scripts/engage.js` — cause shifts on every page at once.
evidence.B8: The deliverable is stated in outcome terms with wide latitude: "You may change, replace, inline, or neutralize layout-shifting code, including third-party-style scripts, as long as the rendered site preserves the same visible elements, styling, and analytics side effects." Two competent agents would plausibly produce materially different artifacts (reserve space vs. inline the script vs. reimplement `engage.js`). The preservation clause and the explicit zero-CLS criterion narrow the gap, so this is not open-ended, but a confident wrong answer — zero CLS achieved by removing the banner or the analytics beacons — reads as complete.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 360` sits in the ~2–8 hour band; per-step orchestration stops are material but do not dominate six hours of work across six routes and two containers.
evidence.C4: The instruction leads with a symptom, not a procedure — "Eliminate cumulative layout shift from the website" — so the first real step is diagnosis: finding which of `engage.js`, the font loading, the promo/announcement banners, or the lazy loaders actually shifts, and by how much. Naming the target directory `/app/barber-shop-site/` does not make the method known.

rows.processRecommendation: library/specializations/performance-optimization/ composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gate: a per-route CLS measurement run plus the DOM-integrity/visual-comparison suite) and n-strikes-escalation.js for the converge-to-zero loop
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent measures CLS on the homepage, traces the shift to `public/scripts/engage.js` and the promo banner, stubs or deletes them to get a clean zero, and declares success — shipping a site that fails the DOM-integrity and visual-comparison checks (`eval/tests/dom-integrity.spec.ts`, `eval/tests/visual-comparison.spec.ts`) because the banner is gone and the analytics side effects the instruction requires preserving no longer fire. The adjacent failure is scope truncation: it verifies zero CLS on `/` and `/services` and never re-measures `/book`, `/gallery`, or `/socials`, where the booking stepper and lazy-loaded feed still shift.
rows.rationale: The strongest case for enforcement here is convergence: CLS is a number the agent can measure itself against an explicitly stated target of zero, per route, which is exactly the shape an iterate-until-target loop with a deterministic gate serves well (B5=3), and the six-hour expert estimate with a three-hour agent timeout means orchestration overhead is not the dominant cost (C2=1). Working against it is shape uncertainty: the instruction is a symptom statement, and nothing about the method is knowable until the agent has profiled the running site and read `engage.js`, so any process encoded up front would be guessing at the remediation phases (C4=3). Ordering is weak — diagnose-then-fix is natural but nothing downstream silently breaks if the agent interleaves them — and decomposability is real but partial, since shared roots in `app/layout.tsx` and the font loading affect every route at once. Drift risk is moderate rather than high: the preservation clause plus the zero-CLS criterion pin the acceptance condition, but the permission to "neutralize third-party-style scripts" leaves a genuine gap in which an agent can reach zero by deleting the very elements it was told to preserve.

rows.name: data-anonymization

evidence.B1: "References to the same underlying entity must produce the same token across all files, including across type-2 history rows, across transitively composing effective-dated subject merges, and across the transitive cross-tenant equivalences asserted in `subject_links.csv`." The equivalence closure over merges must be composed with the closure over subject_links, that combined canonical-entity map must exist before any token is assigned, and tokens must exist before rows are emitted — a chain of at least three steps where doing the work in file order (tokenize as you stream) silently yields plausible-but-inconsistent tokens. Ordering inside one deliverable counts per the profile.
evidence.B3: metadata `expertMinutes: 1440` (24 hours), far above the profile's ~8-hour line and 12x the corpus median of 120; `verifierTimeoutSec: 7200`. The instruction also stacks distinct sub-artifacts (policy interpretation, linkage closure, per-column transforms, bounded-memory streaming writer) that feed each other.
evidence.B5: "Output must be deterministic for a given `--seed`, seeded transforms must change when the seed changes, and peak memory must stay within `--max-memory`" with an explicit `--max-memory 64MB` on the invocation line. The agent can run the tool twice with the same seed and diff, run it with a different seed and confirm change, and measure peak RSS against a stated 64MB finish line — all self-computable quantities with a target, independent of the hidden verifier. Cross-file token consistency is likewise checkable by the agent against its own output.
evidence.B6: The deliverable is one program, `/app/anon.py`. There is mild fan-out in that per-column transform types could be implemented separately, but the central requirement — one consistent token per entity "across all files" — couples every part; the linkage closure cannot be worked independently of the emitters.
evidence.B8: The output contract is pinned hard: fixed path `/app/anon.py`, fixed output dir `/app/output`, and "preserve filenames, headers, column order, row order, and row counts", with per-column behavior dictated by the supplied `/app/policy.yaml` rather than by agent taste. Content is still agent-derived (the token values themselves), so a linkage bug produces a well-formed file that is quietly wrong — but the long constraint list narrows the space of confidently-wrong-but-conforming answers.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 1440` places this well over the profile's ~8-hour band, where mandatory per-step stops are a rounding error against the work. Mirrors B3=3.
evidence.C4: The instruction states a goal, not a procedure, and the method cannot be fixed until supplied inputs are read: `/app/policy.yaml` defines which columns get which transforms, and the schemas of the "related CSV files in /app/input" — the type-2 history tables, the effective-dated merge records, and `subject_links.csv` — determine how the closure and the bounded-memory pass must be structured. It does not lead with a symptom or a complaint, so line 3 does not apply.

rows.processRecommendation: library/specializations/data-engineering-analytics/ composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gates: rerun with identical --seed and diff outputs, rerun with a changed seed and assert transforms differ, assert header/row-count/row-order parity per file, and measure peak RSS against --max-memory)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent implements a single streaming pass that tokenizes each entity id as it encounters it, applying `subject_links.csv` and the effective-dated merges as direct pairs rather than computing their combined transitive closure first; entity A→B and B→C then get two different tokens in two different files, and the type-2 history rows for a merged subject disagree with the current row. The output is byte-perfect on the visible contract — same filenames, headers, column order, row order, row counts — so nothing looks wrong. Compounding it, the naive approach loads the id maps and inputs into memory and quietly exceeds the 64MB `--max-memory` budget, and the agent declares done after eyeballing output shape because it never wrote the seed-stability, cross-file-token-consistency, or peak-RSS checks that would have caught either defect.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is horizon: 1440 expert-minutes with a 7200s verifier timeout puts this at the top of the corpus, and C2 falls to 0 for the same reason, so orchestration overhead is nearly free here. B1 is genuinely 3 — the transitive closure over effective-dated merges composed with the cross-tenant equivalences in subject_links.csv must be fully resolved before a single token is assigned, and an agent that tokenizes while streaming produces output that satisfies every visible structural requirement while being semantically wrong. B5 is unusually strong for this corpus because the instruction hands the agent three self-measurable targets (seed determinism, seed sensitivity, a stated 64MB peak-memory bound) that it can test without the hidden verifier, which is exactly the loop a convergence process enforces. Against that, B8 is only 1 and B6 only 1: the output contract is pinned tightly and the deliverable is one coupled program, so this is not a task where an agent wanders off into the wrong artifact — the risk is silent incorrectness, not sprawl. C4=2 because the policy file and input schemas must be inspected before the method can be chosen, but the work is not diagnostic.

rows.name: distributed-dedup

evidence.B1: The instruction specifies a chained pipeline whose stages each consume the prior stage's output: "Tokenize: text.toLowerCase.split(\"\\s+\")" → "Form the set of distinct contiguous shingleK-grams" → "find all pairs whose shingle-set Jaccard similarity meets the configured threshold" → "cluster them by connected components" → "select one canonical representative per cluster" (clusterId = "the lowest docId in the cluster", isRepresentative = "docId == clusterId"). Candidate generation must be followed by exact-Jaccard verification before clustering, or false-positive pairs silently merge clusters and every downstream clusterId/isRepresentative value is plausible-but-wrong.
evidence.B3: metadata expertMinutes = 600 (10 hours, above the ~8h line and well above the corpus median of 120) and agentTimeoutSec = 18000, far above the 7200 threshold; the instruction itself says "You have 18000 seconds to complete this task." Distinct phases each producing an artifact the next consumes (shingling, candidate pairs, verification, connected components, representative selection), plus a Spark build/benchmark cycle per iteration.
evidence.B5: The agent can measure quantities itself and tell whether they improved: "wall-clock latency", "peak executor memory", "join-operator output rows", "shuffle bytes read and written" are all readable from Spark metrics/UI, and correctness is self-checkable because the spec fully defines the target — "must match a ground-truth all-pairs exact-Jaccard computation by multiset equality" — so a brute-force oracle can be written and compared against on the supplied corpus. Not 3: the stated figures ("at most 1.5x the reference", "at most 1.2x") are ratios to a "hidden human-written reference" the agent cannot evaluate until the verifier runs, so there is no evaluable finish line.
evidence.B6: "Implement your solution by editing /app/submission/src/main/scala/tb/dedup/submission/SubmissionDedup.scala. Do not modify files outside that single source file" — one indivisible artifact. The internal stages (shingling, banding, connected components) are separable enough to be developed and unit-checked one at a time, but they are strictly sequential, not parallel fan-out.
evidence.B8: The output contract is pinned exactly: columns "docId (Long), clusterId (Long, the lowest docId in the cluster), and isRepresentative (Boolean, true iff docId == clusterId)", "Exactly one output row per input doc", singleton and 0-token edge cases spelled out, tokenization given as literal code, and a worked shingling example. The file to edit and the prohibitions ("Do not pull data to the driver, broadcast joins, use Cartesian products, or escape to the RDD API") further narrow the gap. Content — the internal algorithm — is agent-derived, so a wrong result would still be well-formed, but two competent agents cannot produce materially different satisfying artifacts.
evidence.C2: expertMinutes = 600 and agentTimeoutSec = 18000; at ~10 hours of work, mandatory per-step stops and orchestration turns are a rounding error against the build/benchmark cycles this task requires.
evidence.C4: The instruction states the goal in procedural terms — shingle sets, Jaccard threshold, connected components, canonical representative — and the task tags name the conventional method (minhash, lsh, connected_components). It does not lead with a symptom, and no supplied input must be inspected before the approach can be chosen; what is open is the tooling/tuning choice (MinHash+LSH band/row parameters, iterative vs. label-propagation connected components) within a standard domain method.

rows.processRecommendation: library/specializations/data-engineering-analytics/ composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (gate on a self-written exact-Jaccard oracle diff) and library/methodologies/iterative-convergence for the resource-budget tuning loop
rows.vanillaFailureMode: A vanilla agent gets an exact-Jaccard all-pairs (or self-join-heavy) implementation passing correctness on the 10k corpus, sees green, and declares done — skipping the LSH candidate-generation stage entirely, so join-operator output rows and shuffle bytes blow past the 1.2x budgets. The mirror failure is the opposite: it adds MinHash/LSH banding for speed but skips the exact-Jaccard verification of candidate pairs, so false positives silently merge two clusters and every affected row's clusterId and isRepresentative are wrong while the output still has exactly one well-formed row per doc.
rows.rationale: The decisive factors are the chained pipeline (B1=3) and the long horizon (B3=3, 600 expert-minutes and an 18000s agent budget), against near-zero live cost: at ten hours of work orchestration overhead is noise (C2=0), and the method is the conventional MinHash/LSH + connected-components recipe rather than a diagnosis (C4=1). The correctness contract is stated precisely enough — exact column semantics, literal tokenization, worked shingling example, spelled-out edge cases, single editable file — that drift risk is low (B8=1) despite the task's difficulty; difficulty is not drift. B5=2 rather than 3 because the resource ratios are relative to a hidden reference, so the agent can tell whether it improved but not when it has finished. The concrete counterfactual is real and two-sided: vanilla either ships a correct-but-budget-busting all-pairs join or an LSH pipeline missing the exact-Jaccard verification step, and both produce well-formed output that reads as complete.

rows.name: embedding-drift-monitor

evidence.B1: "Fix all the production modules under `/app/drift_monitor/`, not just the alert layer. The statistical and distance utilities have defects too." The pipeline is layered — KS/PSI/MMD statistical and distance utilities feed the detectors, whose outputs feed the debouncer that "emits alerts". Judging the alert layer's behaviour while the underlying statistics are still wrong yields a plausible-but-wrong fix, so the diagnose-bottom-layer-then-upper-layer order matters; one step's output is consumed by the next.
evidence.B3: metadata `expertMinutes: 300` (5 hours) and `agentTimeoutSec: 7200`, which the profile ladder places squarely at 2 (~2-8 hours, or agent timeout at/above 7200).
evidence.B5: "`/app/data/` has the reference embeddings and a handful of `.npy` files for different current-window scenarios" plus stated expected qualitative behaviour ("Stable distributions trigger alerts they shouldn't, real drift goes undetected"). The agent can run each scenario itself and compute quantities — KS/PSI/MMD statistics checkable against canonical definitions or scipy — and tell whether each scenario now behaves correctly, without waiting for the hidden verifier. No stated figure to beat, so not 3.
evidence.B6: "compares incoming embedding windows against a reference baseline using KS, PSI, and MMD tests, then emits alerts through a debouncer" and "The statistical and distance utilities have defects too" — several separately-fixable and separately-checkable units (KS test, PSI, MMD/distance utils, debouncer), but they compose into a single monitoring pipeline rather than N fully independent targets.
evidence.B8: The deliverable is stated purely in outcome terms — "It's broken", "the alert state flickers across windows in ways that don't track the underlying data" — with no output contract, no file list, and no specification of correct debounce semantics (hysteresis window, consecutive-window threshold). Two competent agents would plausibly ship materially different debouncer and PSI-binning implementations that both satisfy the wording. Canonical definitions of KS/PSI/MMD narrow part of the gap, keeping this below 3.
evidence.C2: `expertMinutes: 300` (5 hours) — the profile ladder puts ~2-8 hours at C2=1: orchestration turns are material but do not dominate five hours of debugging work.
evidence.C4: The instruction leads with a symptom, not a procedure: "It's broken. Stable distributions trigger alerts they shouldn't, real drift goes undetected, and the alert state flickers..." The first real step is diagnosis of unseen code. Per the profile this is 3 even though the instruction names the directories (`/app/drift_monitor/`, `/app/data/`) involved.

rows.processRecommendation: library/methodologies/tdd.js composed with library/processes/shared/deterministic-quality-gate.js (a diagnose-then-fix-bottom-up debugging process for layered numerical pipelines is not well covered — worth a library backlog item, closest existing fit is library/cradle/bugfix.js)
rows.vanillaFailureMode: The agent chases the loudest symptom — the flickering alert state — patches the debouncer until the stable-window `.npy` scenarios stop alerting, and declares done, leaving the seeded defects in the PSI binning/epsilon handling and the MMD kernel bandwidth in place; the surface behaviour on the sample scenarios looks correct while the underlying statistics are still wrong, which is exactly what the instruction's \"not just the alert layer\" clause warns against.
rows.rationale: The decisive factor is C4=3: the instruction opens with a complaint about behaviour rather than a procedure, so the entire shape of the work is discovered by reading unseen code and reproducing the misbehaviour — any process encoded up front is a guess about which layers are defective. Against that, the benefit side is uniformly moderate rather than strong: a real layered dependency (utilities → detectors → debouncer) gives B1=2, five expert-hours with a 7200s agent timeout gives B3=2, and the supplied `.npy` scenario files give a genuine self-measurable loop at B5=2. The counterfactual is concrete and is the strongest argument for enforcement — the instruction's explicit \"not just the alert layer\" warning exists precisely because premature-done after fixing the visible symptom is the expected failure — but B8 stays at 2 because the canonical definitions of KS, PSI and MMD constrain most of the answer space even though the debouncer semantics are left open. Overhead is only C2=1 against a five-hour task, so cost is carried almost entirely by shape uncertainty. Net lands close to neutral; the honest reading is that a vanilla scouting pass to diagnose, followed by gated remediation, fits better than either pure route.

rows.name: erp-procurement-planning

evidence.B1: "The final lineage must be either SO -> PO or SO -> MO -> (subassembly MO if needed) -> PO" plus origin rules — "For component POs, enter the related MO reference(s), for example `WH/MO/00010`" — means MOs must exist before component POs can cite them, and SOs before finished-goods POs/MOs. Chained document dependencies, and the buy-vs-make allocation must be computed before any document is created since the margin and capacity checks are portfolio-wide.
evidence.B3: metadata expertMinutes 240 (4 hours), in the profile's ~2-8 hour band; agentTimeoutSec 3600 with an instruction spanning data extraction, optimization, and multi-document creation in Odoo.
evidence.B5: "the portfolio-level new-spend margin stays at or above 28.1% at selling price, while staying within each customer's budget" and "minimizing any new procurement and manufacturing spend" — the agent can compute both the margin and total spend from Odoo prices itself and tell whether a revised plan improved, with a stated figure (28.1%) as the finish line.
evidence.B6: "fulfill new customer orders ... the order requests are available in /workspace/customer_order_requests.csv" gives several orders, but they are globally coupled: "each workcenter's capacity as a hard horizon-wide limit shared across all products", "min/max quantities apply to the entire planning period", "Use one consolidated PO per supplier offer", and a portfolio-level margin. Units cannot be solved independently.
